item.title: Packers vs. Vikings Week 1 TV broadcast map shows wide coverage
item.description: As long as you don’t live in AFC West territory, you’ll be able to see the Packers’ opener on local TV.
item.content:encoded:
When the Green Bay Packers open up the 2026 season against the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, they will do so with the eyes of most of the pro football world upon them. Sunday’s kickoff will take place at 3:25 PM Central time, and the vast majority of the United States will get to see the game on local CBS affiliates.

Week one is a doubleheader week for both FOX and CBS, one of the few weeks when each network gets to show a game in both the early and late Sunday afternoon time slots. CBS stations will carry one of Packers-Vikings or Cardinals-Chargers in the late game, while FOX stations get their pick of Commanders-Eagles or Dolphins-Raiders.

Here’s a look at the initial broadcast map from 506sports.com, with Packers-Vikings in red:

The blue areas will instead see Cardinals-Chargers, which will go out to those two teams’ home markets plus those of the other AFC West teams (the Raiders, Broncos, and Chiefs).

On the call for the Packers’ opening game is CBS’ top commentating team. This year, Jim Nantz will be joined by color commentator J.J. Watt, who is stepping up from the network’s #2 squad to take the place that fellow Wisconsin native Tony had Romo previously occupied. Romo was suspended from CBS programming this summer after being arrested in Milwaukee for OWI, a charge to which he later pleaded no contest, and the network is reportedly negotiating a buyout of Romo’s remaining contract.

This is the first of four games that the Packers are currently scheduled to play in the late afternoon “Game of the Week” time slot this season, though all four of those come in the first nine weeks of the season. Most of the country should expect to see all of those games, except for areas on the west coast that have home teams or divisional opponents also playing in that late time slot.

item.title: Green Bay Packers drop Week 1 depth chart: 6 takeaways
item.description: It looks like TE Jonnu Smith is going to hit the ground running. Also: Brandon Cisse has been named a starter!
item.content:encoded:
The Green Bay Packers updated their depth chart on Tuesday, the first time that they’ve done so going into the 2026 regular season. For the most part, it looks accurate, based on our charting of preseason and training camp rotations, but there were a few things that stood out to me — so I want to talk about them today.

Disclaimer: I’m aware that the Packers probably put little to no mental energy into posting a public “unofficial” depth chart. A few things turned my gears, though.

Running Back

First of all, Kaleb Johnson was listed as the Packers’ third-string running back, which may not be a surprise to some — because he just got here a week ago. Personally, I still believe that Johnson will be the number two ball-carrier in Green Bay while Josh Jacobs is out, as Chris Brooks, who was listed as a second-stringer, is more of a blocking back than a true ball-carrier.

Jonnu Smith

While Johnson just got to Green Bay and seems too low on the depth chart, tight end Jonnu Smith, who was signed by the Packers the same day that the team traded for Johnson, is listed as the team’s second-string tight end behind Tucker Kraft. Smith has played for head coach Matt LaFleur when they were together with the Tennessee Titans, but I thought Smith’s standing going into Week 1 would be more of a question mark, considering he wasn’t signed with anyone this offseason — unlike Johnson, who at least went through training camp with the Pittsburgh Steelers.

It’s going to be tough for the Packers to keep four tight ends active on gamedays (they have to scratch a minimum of five players from their 53-man roster), and Smith and Josh Whyle both overlap as off-ball move tight ends who are primarily pass-catchers. If Smith is already ahead of Whyle, who has been in the program for two years now, then Whyle’s time on the 53-man roster might be long.

Mark Redman, who is sharing the third-string role with Whyle on the Packers’ depth chart, is a blocking tight end, a role that is much more valuable than Whyle filling in as Smith’s potential backup. If I’m guessing today, Whyle is probably going to be inactive against the Minnesota Vikings.

Offensive Line

The Packers’ starting offensive line was listed as Jordan Morgan, Aaron Banks, Sean Rhyan, Jacob Monk and Zach Bako-Bewele (left to right). That’s not really the question right now. It’s whether or not Banks (tendinitis in his knee) and/or Bako-Bewele (coming off a partially torn Patellar tendon) will be able to play a full 60 minutes this week.

Rookie fifth-round pick Jager Burton was listed as the backup center on the depth chart, but don’t make too much of that. If Banks can’t go, it’ll be Burton at left guard (and it’ll be Anthony Belton at right tackle if Bako-Bewele isn’t playing). Even if Banks can play, I wouldn’t be surprised if Burton rotates at left guard.

Defensive Line

We never got the opportunity to see the entire defensive line healthy and active this summer, either on the Family Night broadcast or for preseason games. Because of that, we’re not really sure how the pieces of this puzzle are supposed to fit together.

Devonte Wyatt has been a three-technique (a 3-4 defensive end role in Green Bay’s new scheme) his entire career, so we can plug him in as a starter there. To the surprise of many, the Packers bubble-wrapped Karl Brooks in the preseason and treated him as a true starter, and he’s another 3-4 defensive end type, not a nose tackle body.

On Green Bay’s depth chart, the team listed both Wyatt and Brooks as the starting ends, with free agent signing Javon Hargrave as the starting nose tackle, one slot ahead of Jonathan Ford. It will be interesting to see just how many snaps Hargrave actually plays at the nose this year, as he looked a little out of place filling in that role with the Vikings last season. For what it’s worth, Ford got the “starts” as a true head-up nose tackle this preseason.

The lone third-stringer on the line is camp sensation Anthony Campbell, who will probably be inactive in Week 1, unless Warren Brinson can’t suit up for action due to his calf injury.

Brandon Cisse

Two days ago we reminded everyone that rookie Brandon Cisse hasn’t been named a starting cornerback by the team, but I guess the depth chart release means that that’s no longer true. Yes, Cisse was listed as the starter opposite Keisean Nixon. Nixon has been handling the bulk of the left cornerback snaps with the first-team offense this summer, while Cisse and Carrington Valentine rotated at right corner.

Going into Week 1, I’m assuming that Nixon will play left cornerback full-time while Cisse will get the “start” on the right, even if Valentine rotates in some at the position. For what it’s worth, Cisse is the only rookie starter listed on the depth chart for either the offense or defense.

Returner Options

One of the most inaccurate parts of the depth chart every year is who they list as the team’s returners, but I think the choices they listed as the second-string options behind receiver Skyy Moore actually make sense this time around. On punts, slot receiver Jayden Reed was listed as the number two returner. On kicks, the second-stringer is receiver Bo Melton. Melton, who does a lot on special teams without needing the ball in his hands, is generally the “off-returner” for the team, a role where he’s deep in the backfield on kicks but really fills in more as a lead blocker than a true returner.

My question is whether the Packers would keep Melton as the “off-returner” if Moore ever went down (or was scratched), or if they would have someone else (like a J. Michael Sturdivant) fill in as the off-returner. I’m also unsure if Moore will keep the kick return job when receiver Savion Williams is activated off the injured reserve, but we have a few weeks to figure that one out.

item.title: Titans’ 1st impression vs. the Jets will say a lot
item.description: Do the Tennessee Titans “need” to beat the New York Jets in Week 1?
item.content:encoded:
Many reporters on the Tennessee Titans beat are calling Sunday’s Week 1 matchup versus the New York Jets a “must-win” opener. That is obviously ridiculous on the surface, but there’s some merit to those claims given the context. No team’s season was ever decided in Week 1, but these Titans are attempting to recapture this fanbase’s trust.

The Titans endured consecutive 3-14 seasons in 2024 and 2025. This small-market fanbase hasn’t exactly been forgiving (understandably so). Many late-season games at Nissan Stadium have recently been played in front of meager crowds.

The Titans underwent significant changes this offseason, both on and off the field. While general manager Mike Borgonzi continued rebuilding the roster, a rebranding also occurred. The Titans have three new uniforms, a new logo, and are preparing to open a new stadium in 2027.

For Titans fans to maintain excitement over all the off-field developments, the on-field product needs to warrant it. The Jets have been considered a laughing stock of the NFL (the Titans, too). If Tennessee loses in Week 1 to the Jets, it wouldn’t be shocking if large portions of this fanbase snickered, said “same ole Titans,” before finding other ways to fill their Sundays.

There’s also the revenge element. Head coach Robert Saleh used to coach these Jets. John Franklin-Myers, Jermaine Johnson II, Tony Adams, Solomon Thomas, and Jacob Martin are among those who played for them. Everyone involved wants to prove they’ve moved onto bigger and better things, with Saleh proving he was never the problem.

Realistically, the Titans don’t need to qualify for the playoffs to convince this fanbase they’re on the right track. Fielding a competitive squad that doubles their 2024/2025 win total by finishing 6-11 would highlight direction and growth. Beginning the campaign by beating the Jets would be considered a good-faith gesture.

item.title: Jaguars Reacts Survey: Is the Week 1 matchup against the Browns a trap?
item.description: Who would you rather start at quarterback: Deshaun Watson, Shedeur Sanders, or Admiral Ackbar?
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Jaguars fans and fans across the country.

According to FanDuel Sportsbook, Liam Coen’s Jacksonville Jaguars are 8.5-point home favorites against Todd Monken’s Cleveland Browns. It’ll be the latter’s first game as an NFL head coach, and his starting quarterback is a familiar foe for Jaguars faithful.

Deshaun Watson, who was at one point the obvious successor to Andrew Luck as the king of the AFC South, has soured into one of the worst players in the National Football League. In 2024, he was the NFL’s least efficient passer through Week 7, when he ruptured his right Achilles tendon. Just a few months after he underwent surgery, he rolled his ankle and re-ruptured the same Achilles tendon. The nasty man turns 31 on Monday.

Cleveland’s quarterback sucks. The bigger news is that, for the first time in a decade, reigning Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett will not be wearing orange and brown. The Browns have significant questions across its roster. It wouldn’t be a surprise to see them forecasted for a top-three 2027 draft pick by the middle of the season.

The Jaguars ought to take care of business and start the season 1-0. Do you trust Coen and company to get the job done?

item.title: NFL Super Bowl graphic: Did league predict Cowboys to play in the big game?
item.description: The NFL knew what it was doing with its Super Bowl graphic this year.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL found itself in a curious situation back in January, when some internet sleuths realized the league actually predicted last season's Super Bowl matchup.

It all stems from a graphic the league posted on social media last September. In that graphic, one player from each team was staring at the Lombardi Trophy. The two players closest to the trophy — and in the center of the graphic — were Drake Maye and Sam Darnold … the two quarterbacks who eventually met in the Super Bowl.

That discovery set the conspiracy theorists off. Did the NFL know the eventual Super Bowl matchup beforehand? Did the league orchestrate those two teams playing in the big game?

Well, the league is at it again in 2026. And if the league suddenly does have predictive power, it certainly seems like the Dallas Cowboys and Jacksonville Jaguars will square off in the Super Bowl this season.

Trevor Lawrence and Dak Prescott are right up there. Interesting 👀 https://t.co/aG0GZI4Hrb

— Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) September 9, 2026

If you look closely at that graphic, it's clear that Jagaurs quarterback Trevor Lawrence is front and center, closest to the Lombardi Trophy. On his left, Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott appears to also be in the front row.

So, the NFL spoiled it, right? That's this season's Super Bowl matchup and there's no reason to play the games out?

If you believe that, we have a bridge to sell you.

But also … the league managed to throw a third team into the mix. If you look to Lawrence's right, it certainly looks like Denver Broncos star Patrick Surtain II is also in the front row. Does that mean the league is predicting the first-ever three-team Super Bowl?

If you think about the whole thing long enough, it all becomes very silly. The NFL ran into a happy coincidence last season and now people are going to make way too much of that same graphic a year later.

What is interesting, however, is that the NFL was almost certainly aware of the attention last year's graphic received. Knowing that, the league decided to put out the exact same image this season, but made sure the Cowboys were part of the conversation.

That's not a bad marketing strategy, as putting the Cowboys anywhere near the Super Bowl is sure to elicit a wide range of opinions from fans and the brain geniuses who make a living spewing hot takes for attention.

item.title: Week 1 NFL picks against the spread, predictions for every game: Should the Texans be favored vs. Buffalo?
item.description: The Texans defense had a huge game against Josh Allen last season.
item.content:encoded:
Any good NFL defense has some level of physicality to it. Not many are as violent as the Houston Texans, however.

Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen knows this well. He was sacked a career-high eight times in a 23-19 loss to the Texans last season. It's rare to see Allen not in control, but it was the Texans defense that took over that game.

The Texans have a championship-level defense. There are stars at every level of it. They want to hit the opponent often and make it hurt. But defense doesn't sell as easily as a good offense, especially one with an elite quarterback. That is a reason the Bills are favored by a point in a great Week 1 matchup.

It's hard for people to pick the team with C.J. Stroud at quarterback over Allen's team. But the pendulum has swung too far on Stroud after a truly awful playoff performance against the Patriots. Last season he was 12th in adjusted EPA (expected points added) per play, 15th in success rate and the Texans were 18th in passer rating. That's not great but it's not at a Deshaun Watson level either. He's middle of the road. And with a defense that has a legitimate claim as the best in the NFL, average QB play is good enough to win a lot of games.

The Bills are my pick to win the AFC, but this is a tough matchup for them (and also, it wouldn't surprise me if the Texans are like the 2015 Broncos and ride a great defense to the Super Bowl). The pick is the Texans +1. Either way, this is a really fun matchup for the opener. Unless you're the Bills offense, which has to face a scary and fierce Texans defense to start the season.

Here are the picks against the spread for Week 1 of the NFL season:

Seahawks (-3.5) over Patriots

Hate to be square to start the season, but why aren't the Seahawks a bigger favorite? Seattle pounded New England on a neutral field in the Super Bowl, easily covering a 4.5-point spread, and now the spread is shorter? The Patriots should be better, though being without running back TreVeyon Henderson (ankle) won't help things. The Seahawks did lose some pieces (don't underrate the loss of offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak). However, I still trust them in this spot.

49ers (+3.5) over Rams

Yes, this could be overthinking the Rams' travel decisions. By now we all know what's going on: The 49ers have been in Australia since last week to get acclimated to the 17-hour time difference. The Rams will land a day before kickoff, then leave right after the game. The Rams are a smart organization and they didn't make this decision without thinking it through. Still, it seems hard to believe the Rams will be at their best given an incredibly aggressive travel plan (though others think they'll be fine, as was included in an in-depth report from Yahoo Sports' Jeff Eisenberg). They did something similar for a trip to London and it worked with a 35-7 win over the Jaguars, but this seems like a much different challenge. Taking the points seems like the right move given this is a strange setting for an NFL game. The news that Aaron Donald won't play in the opener isn't too surprising and doesn't change much, though it's another positive for the 49ers.

Titans (-1.5) over Jets

Both teams were awful last season and the Titans — Cam Ward in particular — were uninspiring in the preseason. But here's a pick for the better coaching staff. I trust Robert Saleh to have his team ready. And I'll trust the beat reporters who say Ward looked much better in practices than he showed in preseason games.

Panthers (+3) over Bears

It's rare I'll have a breakdown this basic: The Bears are getting an unbelievable 93% of the bets on the spread at BetMGM. I'm not very high on the Panthers this season and we know their injury issues. But I will not take a road favorite getting 93% of the bets. That's a promise.

Saints (+7) over Lions

This should be a fun one. Here's the test for the Saints, who were good in the second half last season but didn't really beat anyone either. The Lions have holes in the secondary that the Saints should be able to exploit. A touchdown spread seems like too much.

Colts (+3.5) over Ravens

The Ravens' respect makes sense. We have kind of forgotten how good Lamar Jackson is. But what about forgetting how good the Colts were last season before Daniel Jones' injury? There's some trepidation about taking the Colts in Jones' first game action since tearing his Achilles, though practice reports say he looks good. Also, new coach Jesse Minter was a good hire, but are we sure his defensive scheme will take hold immediately? The Colts are the biggest home underdog in Week 1 and that doesn't seem right.

Steelers (-3.5) over Falcons

The Steelers are old, but that might not catch up to them until later in the season. Meanwhile, the Falcons are starting Tua Tagovailoa after a concerning preseason. If the Steelers don't cover in this nearly perfect Week 1 setup, it might be a long season.

Buccaneers (+3.5) over Bengals

Let's roll out two stats. In each of Todd Bowles' four seasons as Buccaneers head coach, Tampa Bay has started 2-0. Meanwhile, the Bengals have been notorious slow starters under Zac Taylor. The Bengals have not escaped September with fewer than two losses since 2021. That all seems relevant to a sneaky fun Week 1 matchup.

Browns (+8.5) over Jaguars

It's not comfortable to pick the Browns, who are starting Deshaun Watson for some reason. But it is a talented team around the quarterback position. The Jaguars were very good last season and could easily cover, but weird things always happen in Week 1.

Commanders (+5.5) over Eagles

We'll see if the Commanders fixed their defensive issues. Working in their favor is this is Philadelphia's first game under new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion. We're going to see Jalen Hurts under center more than we're used to. There could be a transition period, especially as the Eagles learn to play without A.J. Brown.

Raiders (-3.5) over Dolphins

The brave among us will be picking the Raiders in survival pools this week. I don't think oddsmakers have fully accounted for how bad the Dolphins might be this season, even against a Raiders team that earned the first pick of the 2026 NFL Draft.

Cardinals (+10) over Chargers

While there's some discrepancy on official closing lines, Stathead says the Chargers could be the first double-digit favorite in Week 1 since 2012. (Some books have already moved the Chargers down to -9.5.) You just don't see an opening week spread this large very often. The Cardinals will not be good, but they can put up points. They're a backdoor cover threat in every game.

Vikings (-1.5) over Packers

The Packers were favored in this game but the lines have shifted, and rightfully so. The Vikings were 9-8 last season with J.J. McCarthy at quarterback. Kyler Murray is what he is, but that's a lot better than McCarthy.

Cowboys (-3) over Giants

Let's keep this simple: If the Cowboys can't cover here, all that preseason buzz will go right out the window. It's only Week 1 but everyone is ready to dunk on those who were hyping up the Cowboys all offseason.

Broncos (+2.5) over Chiefs

The most worn out line of the offseason was that the Broncos will regress. No kidding. They were 14-3. Only nine teams in NFL history have won 15 or more regular-season games. But the regression police have gone overboard. The Broncos are still a good team, just not one that will duplicate 14-3. Patrick Mahomes is in his first game back from a torn ACL and he's used to playing in the preseason. He didn't this year as he recovered. It wouldn't be that surprising to see Mahomes start a bit slowly, especially going up against one of the NFL's best defenses.

item.title: The NFL stokes conspiracy theories again with Super Bowl 61 graphic
item.description: The 2026 NFL schedule gets underway on Sept. 9, but the NFL already has eyes on February when Super Bowl 61 will be played.
item.content:encoded:
Warning: This article may container spoilers for Super Bowl 61.

In 2025, the NFL posted a graphic on the opening day of the season, with player representatives from all 32 teams walking up to the Lombardi Trophy. The two closest players: Seattle Seahawks QB Sam Darnold and New England Patriots passer Drake Maye.

The two met in Super Bowl 60, with the Seahawks ultimately taking home the hardware, leading some to believe the graphic was less fun, engaging design and more fodder for those fond of tinfoil headwear.

This season, the NFL again stoked some flames of conspiracy: A graphic showcasing players from all 32 teams was posted on the morning of the start of the 2026 season. The two closest to the Lombardi Trophy? Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott and Jacksonville Jaguars QB Trevor Lawrence.

The journey to the Lombardi starts today 👀 pic.twitter.com/AAUDQFDi3l

— NFL (@NFL) September 9, 2026

Could we be in for a Cowboys-Jaguars meeting in Super Bowl 61?

It's not a stretch to believe that the two teams could meet in Los Angeles. The Cowboys' roster is among the best in the NFL, while the Jaguars have continued to stoke Super Bowl aspirations following a 13-4 season that ended in the wild-card round vs. the Buffalo Bills.

But the road to glory has many twists and turns. So, Cowboys and Jaguars fans, don't book those L.A. hotel rooms just yet. Unless you're a fan of a tinfoil hat.

item.title: NFL news, live updates: TreVeyon Henderson out vs. Seahawks, Aaron Donald out vs. 49ers; Patrick Mahomes will 'most likely' start Week 1
item.description: Follow along with the latest NFL news and injury updates approaching Week 1.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to NFL kickoff week, as we await the much-anticipated season opener between the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks on Wednesday — a rematch of Super Bowl LX.

This time around, Patriots running back TreVeyon Henderson will be sidelined. The second-year back has been ruled out with an ankle injury. He hasn’t practiced since Aug. 24. In the season opener, New England will likely lean on Rhamondre Stevenson in the backfield.

Leading up to that matchup, the Patriots agreed to a record-setting four-year, $135 million extension with star cornerback Christian Gonzalez, resetting the cornerback market yet again this offseason.

The league's first-ever matchup in Australia will take place Thursday night between the San Francisco 49ers and Los Angeles Rams.

Reigning Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett will make his debut with the franchise after his blockbuster trade from the Cleveland Browns earlier this offseason. He's missed practice time in training camp and through the preseason with knee swelling but should be good to go. Fans will have to wait at least another week to see the recently unretired Aaron Donald make his return, however, after he didn't travel with the team to Melbourne.

Gonzalez wasn’t the only player who benefited from a massive pay day this week. After it appeared as though Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield would have to play the 2026 campaign on the final year of his contract, he received a last-minute extension, days before the Bucs take on the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 1. Tampa Bay inked the two-time Pro Bowler to a three-year, $165 million contract that takes him through the 2029 season.

item.title: Rams defense gets chance to shine without Aaron Donald
item.description: NFL action is opening up today and get caught up on some Los Angeles Rams news!
item.content:encoded:
Aaron Donald will not be suiting up in Week 1 against the San Francisco 49ers and on one hand, that’s disappointing for fans of the Los Angeles Rams. On the other hand, if the Rams can excel or win without Donald, then that bodes even better for his eventual return to the lineup.

It’s only one game, but it’s a massive opportunity for L.A. to get a divisional win in an international game and set the stage and show this team has what it takes to compete out of the gate.

It’s assumed that this defense should be good with AD, but he won’t be there Thursday so what will this defense be without him? You can bet AD will be watching.

What Aaron Donald’s Week 1 Absence Means for the Rams Defense (si.com)

“While the Rams will be disappointed to not have Donald available, they are playing the long game and want to ensure he is in game shape before he takes the field. The Rams have been preparing without Donald throughout much of the summer, which won’t change how they approach Thursday’s game against the 49ers. This is also a team that’s uniquely built to manage without Donald.

I think what’s cool is you have such confidence in the group that we do have with Kobie, with Fiske, with Poona Ford, with Tyler Davis,” said McVay. “It’ll add value when he’s ready to go, but being two years off retirement, he’s attacked this the right way.”

The Rams do have the depth to manage without Donald against the 49ers. Donald would have certainly added a boost, but the Rams had been preparing all offseason to be without him. It wasn’t until they traded for Myles Garrett that Donald’s return became a possibility. Even then, Donald didn’t make it official until two weeks ago.“

Aaron Donald won’t travel with the L.A. Rams to Australia for Week 1 (ktla.com)

“Defensive tackle Aaron Donald will not travel to Melbourne, Australia, to play in the Los Angeles Rams’ season opener against the San Francisco 49ers.

Donald, who initially retired in March 2024, came out of retirement on Aug. 30. He signed a one-year deal with the team.

While Rams fans will have to wait a bit longer to see Donald back in a Rams uniform, McVay did say that defensive end Myles Garrett, who has been dealing with swelling in his knee, will be “ready to go” in Week 1, according to ESPN.

Garrett, the reigning Defensive Player of the Year who has the record for most sacks in a season (23), is also considered to be one of the best defensive players of his generation. “

Rams release first injury report of Week 1: 2 starters miss practice (ramswire)

Myles Garrett, who will play against the 49ers in the opener, was listed as a non-participant due to his lingering knee injury. Grant Stuard was limited with a hamstring injury, while Jaylen Watson missed practice because of a toe issue. The severity of Watson’s injury is unclear, but there have been no indications that he’s in danger of missing the opener.“

Raheem Morris used to joke that Aaron Donald would ‘get fat when he retired’ (ramswire)

“ESPN’s Sarah Barshop spoke to Morris, asking if the champion coordinator was surprised by Donald’s return.

“No,” said Morris. “I mean, he always stays ready. I used to joke with him and always tell him he’s going to get fat when he retired and he always told me there’s no chance. And he’s right.”

Morris’ final game with the Rams was also Donald’s final contest. In their wild-card loss to the Detroit Lions, ending their 2023 season, Morris would go on to become the head coach of the Atlanta Falcons, while Donald opted to retire.“

Sean McVay and Myles Garrett talk Week 1 expectations ahead of Thursday’s matchup against the 49ers (therams.com)

“Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay and outside linebacker Myles Garrett addressed the media ahead of Thursday’s Week 1 matchup against the San Francisco 49ers. They discuss expectations around the season opener, maximizing every opportunity & more.”

Rams’ Chris Shula names 2nd-year DT who’s been a ‘pleasant surprise’ (ramswire)

““The guy that really stuck out to me was Ty Hamilton,” said Shula on Monday. “I thought he did an awesome job where in camp, it was like Giff (Smith), his position coach, really challenged him to play physical, play fast, play tough. As a rookie, we thought he was kind of thinking and hesitating a little bit too much, and you saw that show up on the tape. He was definitely a pleasant surprise for us, for sure.”

Loaded Rams Carry Highest Ceiling, Highest Stakes in the NFL (sports.yahoo)

“That talent cuts both ways. Health and chemistry will decide whether the Rams hit their ceiling or floor.

Ceiling: 16-1 and Super Bowl Champions

Injuries are the Rams’ biggest threat. They strike randomly and have doomed many Super Bowl contenders. Los Angeles does what it can to prevent that, managing practice schedules and giving rest when needed.“

NFL Power Rankings, Week 1: Cowboys rising after defensive makeover; Bears drop out of top 10 (nfl.com)

“Am I worried about the statuses of Myles Garrett and Puka Nacua? Mildly, although Garrett practiced Sunday, and Nacua appears to be on track to play against San Francisco in the opener in Australia. Oh, and Aaron Donald is back on the team now. No movement for the Rams here, but a big test awaits them Down Under.“

Patriots vs. Seahawks: Five must-know storylines for Wednesday’s 2026 NFL Kickoff Game (nfl.com)

“Our national nightmare is over. After a 212-day break, the NFL officially returns on Wednesday night, with the New England Patriots visiting the Seattle Seahawks to kick off the 2026 season in an instant rematch of Super Bowl LX.

This is the 12th regular-season game between teams that met in the previous Super Bowl, per NFL Research, and the reigning champs are 8-3 in the previous 11 such rematches.

Last we saw these two squads on the same field, Seattle’s defense and running game dominated to the tune of a 29-13 victory. Can the Patriots pull off an upset, with marquee offseason acquisition A.J. Brown in tow this time around?“

49ers catching early breaks — including avoiding Rams’ Aaron Donald (sports.yahoo)

“Kyle Shanahan went out of his way to avoid providing injury updates after the 49ers‘ first practice in Australia, cleverly pointing out that they were a full day ahead of the Rams.

On the flip side, when Aaron Donald was asked about his status after rejoining 11-on-11 practice for the first time this week, all he could muster was a big smile and that he was “feeling good.”

Both sides dropped the act Tuesday.

And the Niners clearly came out in the more favorable position once the dust of the NFC West rivals’ gamesmanship settled. They’ll have Nick Bosa and George Kittle — and will only have to worry about one future Hall of Famer (Myles Garrett) lining up opposite them.“

item.title: Every Former Packer the Team Will See in the 2026 Season
item.description: The team will see quite a few familiar faces on the other side of the field this season.
item.content:encoded:
Last offseason, I ranked the former Green Bay Packers the team would face in the upcoming season based on how much it was gonna hurt to play against them. I specifically ranked them based on pure emotion mixed with how much the Packers could use them at that time. This season, there are a handful more former Packers they’re facing, including some they faced last year and some they haven’t. So this time we’re side-stepping the emotional rankings and looking at every familiar face they’ll see on their schedule.

Let’s get to it!

Week 1: @ Minnesota Vikings
  • RB Aaron Jones
  • LB Eric Wilson

Both of these guys were with the Vikings last year, so it’s nothing new to see them again. Eric Wilson initially signed with the Vikings as a UDFA in 2017, years prior to being one of the only positives on the Packers special teams unit. Aaron Jones was #1 in my ranking last year and would have been high on that list this year taking into account the current Josh Jacobs scenario. Jones will always be the epitome of what the perfect player is: a great player on and off the field. I wish nothing but the best for that man in every facet of his life (except against the Packers).

Week 2: @ New York Jets
  • EDGE Kingsley Enagbare
  • C Josh Myers
  • TE/FB Andrew Beck

Kingsley Enagbare is a player the team will miss this week after only keeping 4 edge rushers on their final roster due to Micah Parsons and Collin Oliver both starting the season with PUP and IR designations, respectively. Not only are they very thin at the position, but they also have a lot of unproven talent (side-eyeing you, Lukas Van Ness) so it’s not the best timing to face Enagbare, who was a solid backup when injuries piled up. Josh Myers they don’t miss at center, but it’d be nice to have Sean Rhyan as a swing lineman with all the shuffling going on amongst the offensive line due to injuries. Andrew Beck, well, he played 32 snaps for the Packers and I had to Google who he was because I don’t even remember him, so no comment needed there.

Week 3: Atlanta Falcons
  • EDGE Za’Darius Smith

Za’Darius Smith recently shared that his main reason for retiring so suddenly last season was to spend time with his mother who is battling Alzheimer’s before she passed away, which was shortly followed by the death of his father and grandmother. All of those things are gutting enough on their own, but all of them happening in such a short period of time is heartbreaking. Therefore, despite him consistently taking shots at the Packers, I will not be making fun of him (again) for the captains patch necklace and Lions Super Bowl ring. Thank you. Onto Week 4.

Week 4: @ Tampa Bay Buccaneers
  • HC Todd Bowles

This will be the first week this season Green Bay won’t see a familiar face on the field. However, Bucs head coach Todd Bowles was a member of the team’s player personnel staff in the ‘95-‘96 season, when the Packers won Super Bowl XXXI, so shoutout to him.

Week 5: Chicago Bears
  • EDGE Jonathan Garvin (IR)

Jonathan Garvin was placed on IR by the Bears in late August and hasn’t played a snap for them. The thing he’s most known for in Green Bay is being cut on his birthday. That’s all I got (plus this terrible meme I made and never got to use, featuring a scene from Role Models).

Week 6: Dallas Cowboys
  • EDGE Rashan Gary
  • DT Kenny Clark

ALRIGHT NOW WE’RE TALKING. When I wrote this last season, it was months before the Micah Parsons trade that sent Kenny Clark to the Cowboys, so he wasn’t on that list. This is also the week Parsons is eyeing as his most “optimistic” return to the field, so there’s lots of reunions going on. The Packers faced Kenny Clark last season in their tie at AT&T Stadium, but this marks Clark’s first return to Lambeau as a Cowboy, along with Rashan Gary, who was traded to Dallas for a fourth-round pick earlier this season. If Parsons is back this week, he’ll surely be on a snap count. However, I fully expect him to still make a bigger impact against his former team in limited snaps than we’ll see from Gary, which is nothing new.

Week 7: @ Detroit Lions
  • No one, surprisingly!
Week 8: Carolina Panthers
  • RB AJ Dillon
  • LT Rasheed Walker

AJ Dillon, a fan favorite to some, has already faced the Packers as an opponent during his underwhelming stint with the Eagles last year. Dillon signed with the Panthers this offseason but, like last season, isn’t expected to see the field much unless injuries pile up in that room. Rasheed Walker, however, is facing the Packers for the first time after the team let him walk without a deal this offseason in favor of their former first round pick, Jordan Morgan. Walker signed a one-year, $4 million contract with the Panthers a few days into free agency. The contract, worth up to $10 million with incentives, is likely a lot less than he was expecting which should make Packers fans feel pretty good about the defense lining up against him.

Week 9: @ New England Patriots
  • WR Romeo Doubs
  • OL Greg Van Roten (yes, he’s still in the league)

First of all, Greg Van Roten is a month older than me so if any of you call him old I am calling the police. Second-of-ly, I wrote in last year’s article about how surprised I was that he was still in the league, then immediately forgot it, I guess because I had the same thought when writing this article. If you can’t tell, I’m stalling so I don’t have to talk about Romeo Doubs. But yeah, Van Roten, that one guy who played for the Packers all those years ago is still in the league at 36 years old (don’t you dare say “old”). He was with the Giants last year, and has been a “just fine” veteran over the last 15 years. PFF ranked him 35th out of 81 guards last season, so, you know, good for him. OKAY FINE! I’ll talk about Romeo Doubs! I hate seeing him for another team. I don’t expect the Packers to miss him on the field despite Doubs being their healthiest WR last season. However, I personally will miss his hilarious and goofy moments the last few years and seeing his comedically giant guardian cap helmet making the most incredible catch you’ve ever seen out of nowhere! Are you happy now?!?

Week 10: Minnesota Vikings
  • See Week 1
Week 11: Bye Week (so here’s some Packers free agents still available)
  • C Lucas Patrick
  • CB Corey Ballentine
  • CB Trevon Diggs
  • CB Robert Rochell
  • DT Dean Lowry
  • DT Mike Pennel (lol)
  • EDGE Preston Smith
  • K Brandon McManus
  • TE/FB Josiah Deguara
  • TE John Fitzpatrick
  • TE/QB Taysom Hill (technically, I guess)
  • TE Marcedes Lewis
  • WR Malik Heath
  • WR Marquez Valdes-Scantling
Week 12: @ Los Angeles Rams
  • WR Davante Adams

WHEW this one’s gonna hurt. The Packers already faced Davante Adams in 2023, when he was in his second season with the Las Vegas Raiders, but this is different. Adams shined last season with a better team and offense than he’s had since being traded from Green Bay ahead of the 2022 season. Davante Adams clearly still cherishes his time with the Packers and even expressed being open to return to the team last offseason before ultimately signing with the Rams. The Rams are a favorite to win it all this year and if the Packers can’t get a ring this season, I hope Adams gets one.

Week 13: @ New Orleans Saints
  • DL Colby Wooden

Wooden was the guy the Packers traded to the Indianapolis Colts for LB Zaire Franklin, who was recently named a captain by the team. The Colts released Wooden during final roster cutdowns at the end of August and the Saints claimed him on waivers the next day. So, looks like the Packers handled that trade pretty well so far.

Week 14: Buffalo Bills
  • None!

But shoutout to Micah Hyde anyway.

Week 15: Miami Dolphins aka Green Bay South
  • General Manager Jon-Eric Sullivan
  • Head Coach Jeff Hafley
  • QB Malik Willis
  • QB Kyle McCord
  • S Zayne Anderson
  • S Jaylin Simpson (Practice Squad)
  • WR Will Sheppard (Practice Squad)

I didn’t include practice squad players in other weeks, but this one felt relevant given the size of the list already. The Dolphins are essentially what the Packers would look like in an alternate universe if the Packers fired their core of GM Brian Gutekunst, HC Matt LaFleur, and QB Jordan Love during this past offseason and replaced them with their respective backups. The haters who have wanted them gone will be taking frivolous notes on the Dolphins over the next few years if the Packers don’t have postseason success.

Week 16: @ Chicago Bears
  • See Week 5
Week 17: Houston Texans
  • CB/PR/KR Tremon Smith

Yeah, I didn’t remember him on the team either. Well, the Packers claimed Smith off waivers in September 2019, waived him on October 14 then re-signed him to the practice squad. He was promoted to the active roster two weeks later, and was waived in December, thus completing his time with the Packers. Anyway, he’s on the Texans now and has had a solid couple of years as a core special teams player for both Denver and Houston.

Week 18: Detroit Lions
  • See Week 7

For those taking notes at home, that makes 19 former players (not counting practice squad), 2 coaches, and 1 general manager the Packers can expect to see this season, assuming nothing changes from now until the end of the season. Here’s hoping the Packers don’t end up missing a single one of them!

item.title: 10 bold predictions for Dolphins 2026 season
item.description: Don’t sleep on some optimism coming from the 2026 Miami Dolphins.
item.content:encoded:
Every other city we go; every other video; no matter where I go, I see the same… NFL power rankings for the Miami Dolphins.  Pick a site… any site… and I guarantee you that you’ll see the Miami Dolphins ranked 32nd.  That negative 3-star restaurant that gave you expired sushi and cold pizza rolls?  They have a higher ranking than the Dolphins and they aren’t even an NFL team.  Expectations are THAT low for the Dolphins.  Everyone expects this team to be the Keystone Cops of the league, being a day off for any opponent to play them.  Even the most optimistic media source out there predicts a high total of 5 wins.  Five.  One, two, three, four, FIIIIIFFFFTH!

Well don’t let the eternal optimist within you listen to the negativity.  The 2026 Miami Dolphins are here to spit in the wind face of all the doubters.  Even if they don’t, they will be a tougher out than people are expecting and maybe even fun to watch.  Ol’ Earl’s here with some bold predictions that will show you how.

1. MALIK WILLIS PROVES TO BE A FRANCHISE QUARTERBACK

I was firmly on board the “Sign Malik Willis” train in March and was incredibly excited when I saw the news he was going to be a Dolphin.  Losing receiver Jaylen Waddle put a dent into the expectations for the signal caller, but the rookie class has stepped up and may give some electricity to the pass catching units.  But they are rookies and rookies have growing pains and lessons to learn and all the other 90s sitcoms tropes.

But that won’t stop me from making this prediction.  I highlighted what I think will be baseline expectations for Willis on Substack.  Now, I’m predicting he will exceed them.  I believe he will pass all the “eye test” criteria.  I also think he will exceed the statistical baseline.  I’m going to go with a 66% CP, 7.7 YPA, 5.7% TD%, and 1.8% INT%.  Using my same dropbacks and attempts totals (595 dropbacks; 476 attempts), that gives him a stat line of 314-476, 3665 yards, 27 TDs, and 9 INTs.  That would yield a passer rating of 100.17.  Looking at 2025 stats, that would put 12th in yards (a grand total of 3 yards behind what Josh Allen threw for), 16th in completion percentage (just under, but in line with Burrow, Herbert, and Love), tied for 6th in TDs thrown, 7th in TD%, and 10th in passer rating.  Those aren’t All-Pro numbers, MVP numbers, or numbers that necessarily stand out.  But given the overall situation, these numbers mean that Miami has found their QB for now and the future. 

2. TIGHT END GREG DULCICH ECLIPSES 1000 RECEIVING YARDS

Dulcich was an afterthought to most fans during the 2025 offseason.  The Dolphins added him to the practice squad in late August, then elevated him in late October.  He played in 10 games, with 3 starts.  He didn’t play until week 8.  He didn’t receive a target until week 9.  He managed to get 33 targets, 26 catches, 335 yards, and 1 TD.  His 33 targets in those 9 games works out to 3.7 or so per game.  In 2026, he does not have any target hogs in front of him.  There is no more Tyreek Hill, Jaylen Waddle, or Darren Waller.  The rookie class looks promising, but they need to prove it.  While that loss of proven talent hurts overall, this gives Dulcich a big opportunity step into a prominent role.  He has already developed some chemistry with Malik Willis and he was making plays in OTAs.  He was quiet in preseason, but the starters didn’t get much playing time.

Can he really get to 1000 yards though?  Last season, his yards per reception average was 12.9.  He had couple of games below 10, but he was mostly above 11.  For the sake of argument, let’s say he averages 12 even.  To get to 1000 yards, he would need 84 receptions.  Based on his catch percentage, he’d need about 108 targets.  On a per game basis, that’s 6.4 targets.  Are you telling me that the Dolphins and all the questions regarding their pass catchers, can’t find 3 more targets per game to Dulcich?  Yes, I know the Dolphins want to be more run oriented.  But last season saw the Dolphins throw the least of any season under McDaniel.  There were still targets to go around.  It can be done.

3. THE OFFENSIVE LINE RANKS TOP 10 FOR THE SEASON

Ah yes… the dreaded profootballfocus talk.  They posted their 2026 OL rankings and surprisingly, the Dolphins were not ranked in the low 40s.  They weren’t even last!  They were in the bottom quartile, however.  But do not fear folks… for I predict that the Miami Dolphins offensive line will have fans turning those thumbs the right way up and that the OL will be a top-10 unit in the league.  In what you ask?  Pressures allowed.  Pressures allowed per game.  Per dropback.  Pass Block Win Rate.  Run Block Win Rate.  Best dressed.  Iron Chef rankings.  I care not for what metric is to be used.  Miami’s offensive line will be top 10 in ALL of them.  Outside of QB, I can’t think of a position or position group more polarizing to Dolphins fans.  It doesn’t matter who they sign, how much they spend, who they draft, or how many players they draft.  The offensive line remains a sore spot.  In 2026, the OL will shut the fans up.  Well… most of them.  Patrick Paul continues to develop into one of the best LTs in the league and was named captain.  Kadyn Proctor locks down the LG spot and strikes fear into the hearts of interior DL.  Aaron Brewer continues his All-Pro run.  Jonah Savaiinaea proves that his rookie season was an aberration and locks down the RG spot.  Either Austin Jackson plays all season and plays well, or Caedan Wallace steps in and fills in seamlessly.  In either case, the OL goes from constant weakness to a source of strength in 2026. And that’s the bottom line…

4. ALL THREE ROOKIE RECEIVERS HAVE A MINIMUM OF 500 YARDS EACH

The Dolphins knew they needed help in the receiver room and the cheap vets they signed weren’t going to be the answer.  They added 3 rookies in the draft.  But at the time, there were serious questions.  The “consensus” board had Caleb Douglas – the 75th overall pick – as a late day three player and was considered a reach.  Chris Bell was coming off an injury that would force him to redshirt his rookie season.  Kevin Coleman Jr. was a slot specialist only and would be stuck behind Malik Washington.  All that “help” was just half-truths and gorilla dust.

Fast forward to now… the “reach” earned his spot in the starting lineup.  Bell hasn’t just returned from injury; he has played real football in a Dolphins uniform.  It was real.  I seent it. Oh… and guess who is the other outside starter at receiver?  Coleman?  Making plays in preseason.  One could very easily argue that the rookies would have shown out more in preseason if the QB play hadn’t been buns.  Well… except for Douglas.  He only played the limited reps with the starters and was stashed for the regular season.

Of course, preseason doesn’t mean anything.  We’ve all seen players show out, then disappear.  But I don’t think this rookie group will.  They will be used and used heavily.  Receiver is a position that generally transitions quickly from college to the pros.  Yeah, learning curve and growing pains and all that.  But this trio is going to be a force.  To the point they each get at least 500 yards. 

Is that too bold?  Following the previous predictions, I have Willis at 3665 yards.  Dulcich is getting at least 1000 of those.  If the rookie trio (assignment for the class: create a nickname for the trio) gets at least 1500 total, that leaves just over 1100 for everyone else.  That’s Washington, Achane, and whomever else.  So no, I don’t think it’s too bold.  I would argue I’m underselling it.

5. CHOP ROBINSON GETS DOUBLE DIGIT SACKS AND MAKES A PRO BOWL

The Dolphins traded Jaelen Phillips last season and released Bradley Chubb this offseason.  That left the edge room bereft of talent.  They didn’t have the financial resources to go out and sign players.  They didn’t really address it in the draft, with the first edge player being a 4th round pick and he is more of a hybrid player.  That put the onus to lead the pass rush group firmly on the shoulders of the former 1st round pick. Chop flashed late in his rookie season but took a step back in 2025.  Now, under the influence of coach Hafley and working with DL coach Austin Clark, the light bulb appears to be turning on and getting brighter.  He has been tabbed as the biggest breakout star of training camp and his best contribution in the very limited preseason action was against the run.  The Dolphins may have something with him now.

A prediction of double-digit sacks isn’t necessarily a bold one, though maybe due to the player.  In 17 games, he just needs to average 0.6 sacks per game to get to 10.  But to make a Pro Bowl?  The range to get into what the normal Pro Bowler is in the neighborhood of 14-16 sacks.  Robinson has some names to leap over if he wants to get into the Pro Bowl, but he earns the spot.

6. JACOB RODRIGUEZ PLAYS AT A DPOY LEVEL

With all the other needs Miami had, the selection of Rodriguez seemed unusual.  They have an All-Pro in Brooks.  They had a good starter in Dodson and added depth with Gay and Harrison.  So why draft another LB? 

Rodriguez is going to prove to everyone just exactly why.  He won the starting spot opposite Brooks in camp and made Dodson expendable.  He will be a tackling machine just like Brooks and will have close to or over the 129 tackles his predecessor Dodson got last year.  Coach Hafley wants LBs that can play in space and cover.  Rodriguez will become a force in coverage, getting himself a couple of INTS.  We already know about his proclivity for punching out the football.  He will force several fumbles this season. 

He won’t win DPOY.  That will go to the edge rusher with the most sacks or if some defensive back has a ton of interceptions.  But his play will put him in the conversation. He’ll definitely be in the running for DROY and winning will again depend on the pass rusher stats.

7. JASON MARSHALL JR. BECOMES OUTSIDE CB1 AND FLASHES LOCKDOWN ABILITY

I don’t think Marshall will be CB1 in the overall scheme.  That’s going to be Chris Johnson.  But Johnson is also going to play inside when the need arises.  Marshall is going to be on the outside primarily.  I think he takes it a step further and becomes a lockdown CB.  His ability to thrive both in zone and in man will make him tough for receivers to deal with.  Quarterbacks will start to look in other places before challenging Marshall.  This frees Hafley and Duggan to move pieces around knowing that Marshall has his side locked down.

The Dolphins felt comfortable enough with him this preseason that he primarily sat out like the rest of the starters.  The secondary is considered a weakness, but that will fade into distant memory as quarterbacks start to avoid Marshall’s side of the field.

This prediction also comes knowing that Marshall has switched his number from 33 (meh) to 4 (🔥).

8. KYLE LOUIS EARNS A STARTING SAFETY JOB BY MIDSEASON

The Dolphins drafted rookie Kyle Louis as a linebacker.  They had listed him on the team site as an ILB.  But with Brooks, Rodriguez, Dodson, and Gay in the mix, it was going to be difficult to find a spot for Louis to contribute and get snaps.  The safety room on the other hand needed lots of work.  Outside of sophomore Dante Trader Jr., who has gotten rave reviews this offseason, the remaining players don’t give you a lot of confidence. 

Louis was drafted to be a hybrid LB/SAF/BIG NICKEL defender that he a lot of teams are now employing.  The Ravens use Kyle Hamilton in a LB/SAF role.  The Seahawks deployed Nick Emmanwori in that role.  The difference was those players are safeties playing LB, Louis is a LB playing safety. 

The Dolphins have now removed all doubt as he is listed as a safety on the team site.  Sully has mentioned him as a player who would play the big nickel.  They are giving him the role that everyone expected.  But… Sully also mentioned him as an impact player on special teams.  That sounds like the transition to safety is going, well… as expected for a rookie changing positions.  His snaps there in preseason were predictably rough.  But I don’t believe the transition takes all season.  By the midway point, Louis will have a firm command of the role and become a starting safety.

At least in the looks with 3 safeties.  Not to backtrack here, but we really don’t know what Hafley will do with the secondary.  They will use both Johnson and Louis in nickel roles, that will likely depend on the matchups.  Regardless, I think Louis proves his worth and forces Hafley to keep him on the field.

9. DJ HERMAN SCORES A RUSHING TOUCHDOWN AND A RECEIVING TOUCHDOWN

Usually, players that get a “tryout” don’t end up making a 90-man roster for training camp.  Teams try players out all the time and nothing ever comes of it.  DJ Herman was an undrafted rookie linebacker from San Diego State with 56 tackles, 1 TFL, and 2 PD in 49 games in college.  That’s not great production.  But the Dolphins gave him a tryout anyway.  As a fullback.  What?  The 6’1”, 242 lb. linebacker was now going to be an offensive player… at an NFL tryout.  The odds were not in his favor.

Herman aced the tryout and earned a spot on the 90-man training camp roster.  But there was no way he was going to make an ACTUAL NFL roster.  Until he did.  Herman got a ton of reps in preseason and played along side the starters.  He did well enough that he survived all the cuts and waiver process.  That is a success story that fans love to hear.  It helps that the player listed ahead of him on the depth chart at fullback, Ben Sims, ended up on IR.  But Herman can only play the hand he was dealt.

There were expected struggles.  He had two targets in the passing game and dropped both.  He did not have a single rush attempt.  The Dolphins kept him because of his blocking and demeanor.  He hits linebackers like… a linebacker.  He is going to help Achane and the run game be very productive this season.  But he likely isn’t going to be a focal point of the offense.  I don’t think he’ll have more than 15 carries all season and no more than about 20 targets.  But he will score at least one time on the ground and one time in the air (where Miami is ALWAYS in control).  That will be quality work for a tryout player.

10. THE DOLPHINS CAN WIN AT LEAST 7 GAMES IN 2026

WHAT?!?!? There is no way the Dolphins can pull that off, right?  They are just too weak on defense and don’t have enough playmakers to get it done.  Well, maybe.  I don’t worry too much about the strength of schedule and all of that.  Teams change year-to-year, maybe not with the severity of what the Dolphins did, but they change, nonetheless. 

Let’s start with the Dolphins themselves and my bold predictions.  It starts with the quarterback.  If Willis plays like I predict, then he will give opponents fits.  If he throws like I predict AND uses the rushing aspect of his game effectively, the Dolphins will control the clock, extend drives, and put points on the board.  If Dulcich and the rookie WRs get what I predict, the offense will not be a weakness.

The Dolphins are also going to be a more physical team, especially up front.  The offensive line is one of the biggest in the league.  The interior OL is the 2nd heaviest in the league at 975 lbs., second only to Dallas.  They are going to move people.  The defensive line is young, but they are going to be physical at the point of attack also.  Phillips is already a solid run stuffing NT and is only tapping into his potential.  This isn’t a finesse team with shiny toys.  This is a team that has a converted linebacker as a fullback.  Lacking talent?  Maybe.  Soft? Not a chance.

Finally, there is a mentality shift.  Yeah, we have heard it all before but look at who is leading; look at the captains.  You have Willis who has been overlooked and written off his entire life.  You have guys with chips on their shoulders and a desire to be great.  You have guys like Paul who stated he could have gone on vacation in his off time but stayed in Miami with the rest of the OL to work.  All these captains are hard-hat, lunch pail players who eat, drink, and sleep football.  Some have their big contracts but they’re still in the building working.  Gone are the self-serving divas who care only about the dollars and “show me the money”.  You think these guys don’t see the power rankings and predictions and the “March For Arch” tanking stuff?  You don’t think that is a driving motivation for them?  Sure, there is some areas that are lacking in overall talent.  But many of these groups have young players just waiting to explode onto the scene.  The safety room may be a weakness now, but why can’t Trader and Louis and Taaffe be answers?  Why can’t these rookie receivers be dominant from the start?  If you told me the starting WR room was Tolbert, Atwell, and some other cheap vet, then I’d be inclined to worry about the talent.  But we haven’t seen what Douglas, Bell, and Coleman can do.

Now… (takes deep breath)… back to the prediction.  I prefer to look at the schedule and see what games are winnable and which are not.  Of course, the Dolphins tend to win some people don’t expect and lose some that people don’t expect.  But barring all that, I see 7 games the Dolphins have a good chance to win.

Division games are always wildcards.  The Dolphins beat the Bills last year for the 1st time since week 3 of 2022.  They won handily too.  But even being hard to predict, I don’t see the Jets as being so much better than the Dolphins that the Dolphins can’t win the game.  In the last 10 years, the Jets have beaten the Dolphins 4 times in 20 tries.  Does anyone remember the last time the Jets won in Miami?  December 28, 2014 (the “home” game loss in 2015 was in London).  I’m not going to tell you the Dolphins WILL win these games, but I wouldn’t bet on the Jets to win either.  That’s 2 possible wins.  And those Willis revenge games against Vrabel could be epic.

Out of division possible wins?  Just need 5.  That would be Las Vegas week 1, Minnesota week 4, Cincinnati week 5, Indianapolis week 10, Chicago week 14, and Los Angeles week 16.  I could give some reasons for why, such as Cincinnati, Minnesota, and Chicago all having 21st or lower ranked run defenses last season.  Or offensive changes such as a new quarterback for the Vikings.  Or a west coast team traveling east to play a 1PM game like the Chargers.

Again, I’m not going to try and pick the ACTUAL games, because there are too many variables week to week.  But I can tell you that there are several winnable games and if Miami’s young talent steps up like we hope, then 7 wins isn’t all that bold of a prediction. Don’t be shocked if/when it happens.

I SAID WHAT I SAID

You tell me… am I close?  Are my predictions way out past the Oort Cloud in terms of closeness?  Personally, I am simultaneously optimistic and pessimistic for the 2026 team.  I don’t have expectations of a bunch of wins, and I really had to talk myself into seven.  But I’m also willing to admit there is a great deal of mystery with this team.  With so much youth and only potential to bank on at quarterback, I can understand why everyone is down on the team.  But I can also see the silver lining of what that potential could be.  It’s gonna be a wild ride for sure.  Let us live the dream while we can.

item.title: Column: Mike Norvell’s coordinator choices might be the final nail in his coffin
item.description: After Florida State lost to Notre Dame by 49 points in November of 2024, Florida State’s athletic department, led by athletic director Michael Alford, decided it would be cheaper to fire almost all of the staff around Norvell instead of the FSU head coach, who had just signed an eight-year, $84 million extension the prior […]
item.content:encoded:
After Florida State lost to Notre Dame by 49 points in November of 2024, Florida State’s athletic department, led by athletic director Michael Alford, decided it would be cheaper to fire almost all of the staff around Norvell instead of the FSU head coach, who had just signed an eight-year, $84 million extension the prior offseason.

So the following day, offensive coordinator Alex Atkins, defensive coordinator Adam Fuller, and wide receivers coach Ron Dugans were all let go. Later in the offseason, legendary FSU defensive line coach Odell Haggins was transitioned into an off-field role.

Norvell’s final three weeks of that season, with the team already sitting at 1-9, were a bye followed by games against FCS opponent Charleston Southern and a bad Florida team. The focus was no longer on 2024, but he had a three-week head start to find new coordinators and reverse the damage in 2025.

The head coach basically tried to hedge his bets. Norvell hired Gus Malzahn, a familiar name who gave him his first big break and who ran a similar offense. On defense, Norvell made a major pivot, hiring defensive coordinator Tony White, who had no prior relationship with him and who runs a 3-3-5 scheme not even seen in FBS football.

Each coordinator brought multiple coaches with them, Malzahn taking offensive line coach Herb Hand and wide receivers coach Tim Harris Jr. from UCF, while White brought defensive line coach Terrance Knighton and safeties coach Evan Cooper from Nebraska.

14 games later, it’s hard to say any of the aforementioned assistants has succeeded in their role.

The Seminoles have lost eight of their last 10 games against Power Four opponents, the latest of which happened in excruciating fashion at home. FSU won the turnover margin (4-1) and time of possession, committed fewer penalties, and yet, walked off Bobby Bowden Field with nothing to show for it after another nothingburger of a performance, a reflection of a whole host of factors, but mostly bad coaching and schematics.

“Tonight, coming off of it, just another close game, a lot of one plays,” Norvell said in his postgame press conference. “You think back through it, some of the explosive plays that we gave up defensively, some of missed opportunities there offensively.”

On the offensive side, expectations coming into the season were low, but the Seminoles have zero juice. Malzahn’s abrupt retirement right before this year’s spring practice forced Norvell back into the spotlight of calling plays, where after two games of evidence, he does not appear to excel anymore. The Noles were an unbelievable 2-of-15 on third downs on Monday. FSU did go 2-of-4 on fourth downs, but the decision to go for it the first time, 4th-and-1 at its own 45, culminated in one of the worst play calls of the game, resulting in a turnover on downs and, shortly after that, a 14-7 deficit.

Malzahn had an up-and-down lone season calling plays for FSU’s offense, but the flatline that has been the first two games back under Norvell’s playcalling make one crave the Malzahn roller coaster.

White’s hire finally marked a departure from the norm and a move toward something new. He brought an honest energy to his press conferences and was billed as a “mad scientist” by all who talked about him. Arriving with him were two coaches with NFL backgrounds, Knighton and Cooper, to help teach his new scheme to the holdover coaches and new players. The stats backed him up, as Nebraska finished top-20 in the country in total defense in 2024.

But not everything on paper works in practice.

Even though White’s unit forced three turnovers on Monday, they were shredded. The Seminoles allowed almost 600 yards of total offense, 8.7 yards per play and gave up 8 of 14 third-down conversions.

If those stats are not bad enough, look at the explosive plays from the Mustangs, who had three receptions of 50-plus yards. Even in year two, none of the players appear understand the scheme, and coverage busts remain an issue.

Worst of all, though, all of the players White banked on taking a step forward have not lived up to expectations. The defensive line, coached by one of his disciples, Knighton, does not seem to have anyone above average. After Daniel Lyons went without a stat on the scoresheet last week, Mandrell Desir, one of the highest-paid players on the Seminole roster, did not record a tackle against SMU. Of the seven Seminole defensive linemen with 10 or more pass-rush snaps, not one had a pass-rush grade over 65.0 according to Pro Football Focus. Florida State did not record a sack either, meaning that Knighton has as many cryptic Twitter posts since the start of fall camp (3) as FSU has sacks this season.

On the backend, none of the safeties are on the same page, even after Norvell said the defense spent all week stressing communication, to the point where FSU played crowd noise on defense in practice to get familiar with a loud stadium. Even though Ashlynd Barker played well against SMU, the coverage busts and poor angles stem from bad coaching and execution. Safeties CJ Richard Jr. and Ma’Khi Jones, two transfers brought in this offseason because they fit the scheme, played over 59 snaps each yet both had a coverage grade under 60 according to PFF (below average). Richard had the highest total defensive grade of the two at 60.3.

The Seminoles lost the game on defense because the front seven, which the coaching staff praised all season, couldn’t generate pressure, forcing White to blitz and opening up massive coverage busts and space on the back-end.

As seen across the country on a weekly basis, getting the coordinators right can solve many problems. Norvell had the chance to quickly dig himself out of his 2024 hole by landing two exceptional play callers. Unfortunately for him, those decisions should be the last major choices he makes before what appears to be his inevitable firing.

item.title: A look back at the history between the Saints and Lions
item.description: How did it all start for these two team teams?
item.content:encoded:
The New Orleans Saints will open the 2026 season on the road Sunday afternoon against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field.

The Saints and Lions first met on Nov. 24, 1968, at Tiger Stadium in Detroit, with the game ending in a 20-20 tie. Since then, the teams have met just 28 times, with New Orleans holding a 14-13-1 advantage in the all-time series.

The last time these teams faced one another, Detroit came away with a 33-28 victory in New Orleans in 2023, giving the Lions the edge in the most recent chapter of the series.

The Saints enter the 2026 season looking to improve on their 6-11 record from a year ago. Following another losing season, New Orleans made several changes during the offseason in an effort to turn things around and return to playoff contention.

With a new season comes renewed optimism, but that optimism will ultimately have to translate into wins. The Saints believe they have added enough talent to compete in the NFC South, and Sunday’s opener against Detroit provides their first opportunity to show they are ready to take the next step.

The Lions enter the season with a similar goal after a disappointing 2025 campaign. Detroit finished 9-8 and missed the playoffs, a significant step backward after going 15-2 and earning the NFC’s No. 1 seed in 2024.

Despite that disappointing finish, Detroit remained one of the NFL’s most productive offensive teams, averaging 28.3 points per game, which ranked fourth in the league. The Lions will look to carry that offensive firepower into 2026 while putting last season’s struggles behind them.

For both teams, Sunday’s matchup represents a fresh start and an early opportunity to set the tone for the season.

Kickoff is at 12:00 pm and the game will be broadcast on FOX with Kenny Albert (play-by-play), Jonathan Vilma (color analyst) and Megan Olivi (sideline)

item.title: What you need to know about the Giants, Cowboys Week 1 opponent
item.description: Get caught up on the Cowboys opponent
item.content:encoded:
Week 1 is finally upon us, and with that comes the resurrection of professional football for the 2026 season. This year the Cowboys don’t have to wait long to renew one of their oldest rivalries.

Dallas opens the 2026 season Sunday night against the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium, and while plenty about this matchup will look familiar, the team the Cowboys face isn’t quite the same one that went 4-13 a year ago.

The Giants spent the offseason remaking their coaching staff and loading up on young talent. Now they get to see whether all that change can translate into wins. So, before the Cowboys and Giants kick off Sunday night, here’s a quick look at what has been happening in New York.

The Giants added plenty of new faces

The Giants overhauled their coaching staff. John Harbaugh takes over the team, giving the franchise a former Super Bowl winner with a large reputation in the NFL. Harbaugh’s teams are physical, and they will run the football. His presence is the big headline change in New York for the 2026 season.

New York was also busy in free agency, bringing in several players with ties to Harbaugh’s former team in Baltimore while also addressing some obvious roster weaknesses. Among the notable additions were linebacker Tremaine Edmunds, cornerback Greg Newsome II, defensive tackle DJ Reader, tight end Isaiah Likely, fullback Patrick Ricard and punter Jordan Stout. The Giants also added receiver Darnell Mooney and safety Jevon Holland to finish a furious free agency period for the G-men.

Then came the draft. The Giants had two picks in the top 10 and used them on Ohio State linebacker Arvell Reese at No. 5 and Miami offensive lineman Francis Mauigoa at No. 10. They added Tennessee cornerback Colton Hood in the second round and Notre Dame receiver Malachi Fields in the third, rounding out what could be a nice mix of young and veteran talent on the roster.

Reese could stand out as one of the best players out of the 2026 draft. At Ohio State, he totaled 69 tackles, 10 tackles for loss and 6.5 sacks in 2025. Harbaugh has said the plan is to move Reese around, allowing him to line up inside, attack gaps and rush off the edge alongside Brian Burns, Abdul Carter and Kayvon Thibodeaux, making them, on paper, one of the most athletic defensive lines in the NFL.

This is Jaxson Dart’s team

The Giants also enter 2026 with a second-year quarterback taking over the offense. Jaxson Dart is the starter, with veteran Jameis Winston serving as his backup. Dart’s development is arguably the biggest variable in determining how much better New York can be this season, but with the reins firmly in his grasp this year and a full offseason program behind him, the next step could be a big one for the second-year pro.

Last year Dart threw for 2,272 yards on 216 completions (63%) with 15 touchdowns and five interceptions. Dart also showed he was a capable, dangerous scrambler. Adding 86 carries for 487 yards and nine touchdowns, and with all the offensive additions and the return of Cam Skattebo, Dart will have plenty of help around him in 2026.

Despite injury recovery, Malik Nabers should still be an offensive centerpiece

If there is one Giants offensive player Cowboys fans don’t need an introduction to, it’s Malik Nabers. After torching Dallas last year in week two for 167 yards on nine catches and two touchdowns, Nabers is looking to continue his dominance against his divisional foes. However, the second-year receiver is returning from the ACL injury that ended his 2025 season, and his availability and effectiveness will be one of the biggest storylines Sunday night. New York released longtime receiver Darius Slayton just days before the season, leaving a receiver group built around Nabers, Mooney, Beckham and rookie Malachi Fields.

That makes Nabers even more important. The Giants also have some interesting options in the backfield. As mentioned earlier, Cam Skattebo is back from his scary ankle/leg injury that derailed his rookie season, while Najee Harris, Tyrone Tracy Jr. and Devin Singletary give New York plenty of options depending on the situation in the run game.

The defense could be the biggest problem

The Giants’ defense was a major weakness last season, particularly against the run, coughing up 145.3 rushing yards a game, good for 31st in the NFL, but there is considerably more talent on that side of the ball now.

Burns and Thibodeaux are veterans, while Abdul Carter enters his second season and Reese gives New York another versatile weapon. Edmunds adds experience inside, while the secondary received a significant facelift with the additions of Newsome and Holland.

And there is an interesting Cowboys connection here. Chauncey Golston, who spent the first five seasons of his career in Dallas, is now with the Giants and is listed as a starting defensive end on New York’s Week 1 depth chart.

The Giants are also expecting a bounce-back from cornerback Deonte Banks, who has won a starting spot opposite Greg Newsome heading into Week 1. This isn’t the same defense Dallas saw last year. Like the Cowboys unit that struggled last year, this defense should and could improve a lot.

So, how did the Giants look in the preseason?

Pretty good. New York went 2-1, losing its preseason opener to Minnesota 13-10 before bouncing back with a 26-3 win over Miami and a 23-6 victory over the Jets. The finale against the Jets was particularly clean. The Giants held New York scoreless after its opening drive, while rookie kicker Dominic Zvada made three field goals, including a 53-yarder. Tyrone Tracy Jr. and Xavier Gipson also scored touchdowns.

Of course, preseason results don’t tell us much about what a team will actually be in September. But for a first-year coaching staff, going 2-1 while establishing the physical identity Harbaugh has talked about is at least a decent starting point.

The Cowboys have plenty of history on their side, however

Dallas has dominated this rivalry historically, holding a 78-48-2 regular-season record against New York and winning 16 of the last 18 meetings. The Cowboys are also 11-1 against the Giants when the two teams have met in Week 1. Even if the most recent meeting didn’t go Dallas’ way, the Giants are facing some daunting and one-sided historical numbers against Big D.

While this is still the Giants, it isn’t exactly the same Giants the Cowboys have beaten up on over the last decade. New coach. New defensive pieces. A different offensive philosophy. A second-year quarterback. And a roster that looks considerably more like the kind of team Harbaugh wants to build. For the Cowboys, Week 1 is the first chance to find out whether all of that change actually made New York better.

And that’s really the question entering Sunday night: How much of the new Giants will show up when the games finally count? Will it be enough to beat history?
