item.title: Bills Mafia, who are we rooting for in Week 1?
item.description: Rooting Interests before we know what our rooting interests are
item.content:encoded:
We made it, Bills Mafia.  

The NFL season kicks off tonight. We have hours and hours of meaningful football ahead of us this weekend, and we definitely aren’t going to watch it without choosing sides. We’re the number one fan base in the league, after all. 

There’s just one problem: We don’t really know who all of our enemies are yet. We know we will almost never root for the AFC East, but beyond that, there are no playoff scenarios to calculate, no strength-of-victory tiebreakers to chase, and no late-season games where we suddenly find ourselves cheering for a team we’ve spent the previous four months making fun of. 

Rooting Interests is almost ridiculous in Week 1, but we’re Bills fans, so of course we’re doing it anyway. 

We don’t know which AFC teams will be standing between Buffalo and the Number 1 seed in January. We don’t know which teams will be fighting for the final wild-card spots, which supposedly good teams will fall apart, or which team nobody is thinking about right now will become a problem. 

But we still need somebody to root for; so, until the 2026 season gives us enough information to know exactly what Buffalo needs, we’re going to make our own rules. 

Think of this as the early-season Rooting Interests constitution:  

  • Always root for the Bills 
  • Build Buffalo’s tiebreakers for later.  
  • Knock last year’s AFC division winners down a peg.  
  • Push struggling AFC teams away from premium draft picks.  
  • Keep the best draft picks in the NFC.  
  • When two irrelevant NFC teams play, root for the better team to win and the worse team to lose. 
  • When the rules conflict, Buffalo’s 2026 interests come first.  
  • And, above all else, never forget that the Patriots, Dolphins and Jets can lose every single game they play, and we won’t feel even a little bit bad about it. 

One important reminder before we get started: These are rooting interests, not predictions. We aren’t picking who we think will win, who Vegas favors or even necessarily who we think is the better team. We’re simply deciding which outcome Bills Mafia should want based on what could help Buffalo — now, later or somewhere way down the road. 

AFC East

Buffalo Bills over Houston Texans 
Seattle Seahawks over New England Patriots 
Tennessee Titans over New York Jets 
Las Vegas Raiders over Miami Dolphins 

Rest of the AFC 

Cincinnati Bengals over Tampa Bay Buccaneers 
Batlimore Ravens over Indianapolis Colts 
Cleveland Browns over Jacksonville Jaguars 
Atlanta Falcons over Pittsburgh Steelers 
Los Angeles Chargers over Arizona Cardinals 
Kansas City over Denver Broncos 

NFC vs NFC games 

LA Rams over San Francisco 49ers 
Chicago Bears over Carolina Panthers 
Detroit Lions over New Orleans Saints 
Green Bay Packers over Minnesota Vikings* 
Philadelphia Eagles over Washington Commanders 
Dallas Cowboys over New York Giants 

*This one doesn’t really matter. Buffalo plays them both. They had a half game separating them in last year’s final standings. But I’m petty, and the Vikings made me mad, so I’m going Green Bay. 

Are we going to look back at some of these picks in October and wonder what we were thinking? Almost certainly. There’s a decent chance one of the teams we’re rooting for this week becomes the team we need to lose games in December. 

But that’s a problem for future Bills Mafia. Right now, we have a full slate of football, a handful of rules, and absolutely no intention of sitting through any of these games without knowing who we want to win. 

Soon enough, we’ll be digging through strength of victory, conference records, and playoff scenarios looking for every tiny advantage Buffalo can get. The rules will change. The priorities will shift. And the standings will eventually tell us who the real enemies are. 

The math will come later. 

For now, we pick sides.

item.content:encoded:
The Villanova Wildcats’ defense has started the year off with mixed results after a rough loss to William & Mary, followed by a strong performance against Bucknell. The defense seemed to struggle with W&M’s mobile quarterback as he extended plays with his legs. This defense plays aggressively, which can bite them in some moments. The Cards will have an opportunity to improve on some of the things that worked against Ole Miss.

Ratu Delano Navoti heads things up for the defensive line at his nose tackle spot. He has two sacks this season with 14 pressures overall. At 6-3/290, he is undersized for his position, but he plays with good quickness, which shows up when he rushes the passer. The Cards will have an opportunity to clear space for the running game if they can control the middle of the line.

Nova is also undersized at defensive end for their 3-3-5 scheme. They don’t have many players over 255 pounds, but that hasn’t been a major issue with their run defense. They are only allowing 2.7 yards per carry on the season, with no big explosive plays allowed in the running game. Ugo Nwotite is the player to watch out of this group. He is a good pass rusher with 7 pressures on only 49 snaps.

The star of this defense is Omari Bursey at linebacker. He leads the team with 29 tackles and 4.5 tackles for loss. He does it all for this defense as their best “downhill” defender while also being able to make plays chasing down plays at the second level. Bursey also had a very nice interception against Penn State last year, so this moment won’t be too big for him. It’s a small sample size, but I would not be surprised to see him hit the portal and end up at the FBS level next season.

The Nova secondary has not had a great start to the season. Opposing teams are completing 65% of their passes, with their starting corners being beaten multiple times. Mikey Allen and Newton Essiem will provide the Cards with an opportunity to open up the passing game early after they struggled to start the Ole Miss game. This group has been the weak link in the defense so far.

item.title: Steelers 2026 season predictions: Record, award winners, and more
item.description: Football is back, so the BTSC staff are giving you their takes on the Steelers, the AFC North and the rest of the NFL.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL’s 2026 season gets underway tonight with a Super Bowl matchup between the Seattle Seahawks and the New England Patriots. The Steelers season won’t be long behind, with Pittsburgh set to face off against the Falcons during the early slate of games this Sunday (1 p.m. EST).

With anticipation mounting, we at BTSC decided to bring back our staff roundtable and discuss what we’ll be watching this season with the Steelers, and what else we’re thinking about the rest of the NFL. While we’re certain to be surprised by some outcomes of this season — this is why you play the games! — it’s always fun to look back at the end of the season on how we thought the season would go, and see where we were on the right track and where we were hilariously off base.

After you’ve read our selections, be sure to sound off in our comments with your takes! We look forward to reading your thoughts about the upcoming seasons and talking ball with the BTSC community.

Here we go Steelers!

Which Steeler are you most excited to watch this season?

Mike Nicastro: Call me crazy, but my choice is Aaron Rodgers. How often will we get the chance to watch a top-five quarterback of all time have his swan song with the team you root for? I’m excited about the additions to the offense, as well as reuniting with his former coach, Mike McCarthy. It will be entertaining – for better or for worse.

Joey Bray: I am very much looking forward to seeing Nick Herbig in what should be an expanded role. Every season Herbig has been in the league, his sack total has increased. This season should be no exception, given the fact that Herbig signed a massive extension in the offseason. I would not be shocked if Herbig leads the Steelers in sacks this season.

Ryland Bickley: Jaylen Warren. He’s long been one of the league’s most underrated running backs, in my eyes, and I’m excited to see what he can do in Mike McCarthy’s offense.

Ryan Parish: I will echo this answer a little further on in this exercise, but the Steelers selected the exact two players I wanted them to in this year’s draft when they took Max Iheanachor and Germie Bernard with their first two picks. I think both will eventually take over important roles for the team during the season, and I will eagerly await their debuts.

Jarrett Bailey: I look forward to Aaron Rodgers shutting up a lot of people again. Not projecting a top-10 quarterback season by any means, but he’s still a top-20 guy.

What is the most interesting storyline for this year’s team?

Ryland Bickley: It’s abstract, but can the new coaching staff finally give the Steelers the jolt the team has seemingly been missing the past several seasons? In more concrete terms, that’s innovation on both sides of the ball and maybe some rising stars on the coaching staff. It’s also the roster’s most highly-paid position groups actually living up to their potential. And most importantly, will the team look like it’s actually building towards eventual Super Bowl contention, not floating in a perpetual state of wild card losses?

Ryan Parish: The Steelers are a team trying to straddle two different timelines. They want to “win now” for their older core (Rodgers, Heyward, Watt, Ramsey), but they’re also keeping 11 rookies and have several other young players we’d like to see make the leap this year: Derrick Harmon, Yahya Black, Troy Fautanu, Roman Wilson, Payton Wilson, Mason McCormick, Jack Sawyer, Carson Brueneer. Nick Herbig and Keeanu Benton just got large extensions — and Joey Porter Jr. will either get one just under the wire before Sunday or potentially be a franchise tag candidate next year — can they continue to get better and pay off those deals? While the Steelers may have the “oldest roster” on average in the NFL (27.1 years old), that list of players I reeled off is a significant chunk of the roster. How many of those players can take a major step forward in their development this year? The answer will tell us how viable this roster’s construction is as the team enters the post-Rodgers era in 2027.

Jarrett Bailey: If the Steelers are a playoff team again, the best storyline will be how everyone who swore Mike Tomlin was the only thing good about the Steelers and the only reason they win games will have egg on their face. Defensively, they’ll be better. Offensively, they should be better. This is a team that has all the tools to make it to the postseason.

Mike Nicastro: TheRodgers-McCarthy reunion is intriguing, of course, but I’ll go with the aging defense. When will Father Time find them? Cam Heyward and Jalen Ramsey will eventually hit a wall – and TJ Watt isn’t getting any younger. Do they have a stellar year left in them collectively?

Joey Bray: How different does this team look under Mike McCarthy? While the Steelers return much of the same talent that won them the division last season, how differently will the team perform week-to-week and respond to adversity under a new head coach? I am very intrigued to see a new era of Steelers football under Mike McCarthy.

Who will be the Steelers team MVP, Defensive Player of the Year, and Offensive Player of the Year?

Jarrett Bailey:

  • Team MVP: Aaron Rodgers
  • DPOY: Nick Herbig
  • OPOY: Jaylen Warren

Ryland Bickley: 

  • Team MVP: Troy Fautanu
  • DPOY: TJ Watt
  • OPOY: Jaylen Warren

Mike Nicastro:

  • Team MVP: Aaron Rodgers 
  • DPOY: TJ Watt
  • OPOY: DK Metcalf

Joey Bray:

  • Team MVP: Nick Herbig
  • DPOY: Cam Heyward
  • OPOY: Zach Frazier

Ryan Parish: 

  • Team MVP: Zach Fraizer
  • DPOY: Cam Heyward
  • OPOY: Michael Pittman Jr.

11 rookies made the roster. Who is the Steelers Rookie of the Year?

Ryan Parish: Anyone who followed my draft coverage knows I was a big fan of both the players the Steelers selected with their first two picks: Max Iheanachor and Germie Bernard. Iheanachor likely won’t start for the first part of the season, but I believe Bernard is already putting pressure on the coaching staff to play him with how he looked in the preseason. His ability to get open quickly underneath, as well as create yards after the catch, pairs well with the type of quarterback Aaron Rodgers is at this point in his career. That’s why I have Bernard eeking out this honor.

Joey Bray: One of the biggest surprises of the 53-man roster was the Steelers keeping Eli Heidenreich as the team’s RB3. Not only will Heidenreich be the team’s third running back, but he will also be the personal protector on special teams. I would not be shocked to see Heidenreich get some runs as a return man this season as well. It’s pretty obvious that the Steelers coaching staff sees Heidenreich as someone who can play anywhere on the field, and it would be silly to keep him on the roster and not put the ball in his hands. Despite being a seventh-round pick, he has one of the clearest paths to immediate production of any Steelers rookie. I think he is an underrated pick for Steelers rookie of the year.

Mike Nicastro: I think Max Iheanachor will take over the starting right tackle spot early and won’t let it go. Germie Bernard will come on late, but “IMax” will have the biggest impact.

Ryland Bickley: It appears Max Iheanachor is on the fastest track to a starting gig this season of the team’s rookie class, and if he continues on what has been a promising trajectory this summer, he should quickly establish himself as the roster’s top right tackle. If the Steelers hit on the Iheanachor selection, it’s an easy pick for this award.

Jarrett Bailey: Germie Bernard. He’ll get quality snaps very early on and be an important part of the passing game.

What’s the Steelers’ final record, and do they make the playoffs?

Jarrett Bailey: 11-6, fifth seed in the AFC.

Joey Bray: 8-9, missing the playoffs.

Ryan Parish: 11-6. Yes, they lose the division on a tiebreaker, but sneak in as the 7th seed by one game, thanks to the AFC West cannibalizing itself.

Mike Nicastro: 10-7. Yes, as the fifth seed.

Ryland Bickley: 10-7, seventh seed – they sneak into the playoffs yet again.

What will be the final standings in the AFC North?

Joey Bray:

  • Ravens: 11-6
  • Steelers: 8-9
  • Bengals: 7-10
  • Browns: 3-14

Ryland Bickley:

  • Ravens: 11-6
  • Steelers: 10-7
  • Bengals: 10-7
  • Browns: 5-12

Mike Nicastro:

  • Bengals 11-6
  • Steelers 10-7
  • Ravens 10-7
  • Browns 4-13

Jarrett Bailey:

  • Bengals: 12-5
  • Steelers: 11-6
  • Ravens: 9-8
  • Browns: 5-12

Ryan Parish: 

  • Ravens 11-6
  • Steelers 11-6
  • Bengals 10-7
  • Browns 2-15

NFL’s surprise team that’s better than expected?

Ryan Parish: Every year, the NFL seems to have at least one team go from worst to first in their division. This year, my pick for that is the Saints, who I have winning the NFC South. I like the offense that head coach and playcaller Kellen Moore has brought to New Orleans, and I think Tyler Shough is talented enough to play the quarterback position at an above-average level, even if true superstardom might be out of his reach. The offensive line has quickly been rebuilt and isn’t talked about enough. The defense has some intriguing pieces like a finally arriving Chase Young, as well as some underrated players like Jonas Sanker, Kool-Aid McKinstry, and Justin Reid.

Jarrett Bailey: Since Ryan already said my darling NFC team in New Orleans, I’ll say the Titans in the AFC. Love the defensive additions in John Franklin-Myers, Alontae Taylor, and Cordale Flott. Cam Ward has actual NFL receivers to throw to in Carnell Tate and Wan’Dale Robinson, and the coaching staff is one I’ll hesitantly believe in. Robert Saleh will have the defense playing at a respectable level, and Brian Daboll is a proven floor-and-ceiling raiser with quarterbacks.

Ryland Bickley: The Vikings and Saints are my top choices as well, but to throw a more obscure pick out there, I think the Panthers remain a little underrated after winning the NFC South last year (at 8-9, to be fair) and putting up a good fight in the playoffs. That said, if Bryce Young can be solid in 2026, Carolina has a better starting lineup than you might think and could be a tough team to beat, even if I don’t see them making the playoffs.

Mike Nicastro:  The Vikings. I think Minnesota will make a stunning run to the NFC Championship Game.

Joey Bray: With Ryan and Jarrett taking a few of my favorite “worst to first” candidates, I’ll take a bit of a different route here. I have the Houston Texans going into the playoffs as the top seed in the AFC. On most major sportsbooks, their win total is set at 9.5, which I think is entirely too low given they have arguably the best defense in the entire league. I’m banking on CJ Stroud to have a bounce-back season and for the Texans to be one of the very best teams in the league throughout the regular season.

8. Who wins NFL MVP?

Ryland Bickley: It feels like we’re due for another Josh Allen/Lamar Jackson debate in the MVP race, but my less-obvious pick is Dak Prescott.

Joey Bray: Give me the Iceman, Caleb Williams, to win the award. Everyone seems to think the Bears are a prime regression candidate, but I think everyone is underestimating just how lethal that offense will be in Chicago with Ben Johnson in charge and Williams throwing the ball.

Ryan Parish: I’ll continue my little rivalry debate with Joey over who really is the best quarterback from the 2024 class: Drake Maye. He was MVP runner-up last year on a team with a less-than-perfect line and where his top two receivers were the now-traded-away Keyshonn Boutte and Mack Hollins. This offseason, the Patriots continued to invest in the offensive line and brought in AJ Brown to be the top wideout. If Maye can play even better than last year with a bona fide alpha receiver at his disposal, MVP is within reach.

Jarrett Bailey: Joe Burrow throws 50 TDs and wins MVP.

Mike Nicastro: Dak Prescott.

Who are the OPOY and DPOY?

Jarrett Bailey:

  • OPOY: Ja’Marr Chase
  • DPOY: Myles Garrett

Mike Nicastro:

  • OPOY: Jahmyr Gibbs
  • DPOY: Myles Garrett

Ryan Parish:

  • DPOY: Will Anderson Jr.

Ryland Bickley:

  • OPOY: Jahmyr Gibbs
  • DPOY: Will Anderson Jr.

Joey Bray:

  • OPOY: Puka Nacua
  • DPOY: Myles Garrett

Coach of the Year?

Ryland Bickley: Kellen Moore (Saints)

Joey Bray: Ben Johnson (Bears)

Ryan Parish: Liam Coen (Jaguars)

Mike Nicastro: Kevin  O’Connell (Vikings)

Jarrett Bailey: Brian Schottenheimer (Cowboys)

Division winners and the playoff field

What’s your Super Bowl matchup, and who is winning?

Ryan Parish: Winner of the Seahawks/Rams playoff game (I’ll say Seahawks, but it’s a coin flip) beating the Jaguars.

Ryland Bickley: Rams over Texans

Joey Bray: Rams over Chiefs

item.title: Who will be the Detroit Lions’ breakout player of 2026?
item.description: Making our 2026 Detroit Lions predictions for Breakout Player of the Year.
item.content:encoded:
Because the Detroit Lions didn’t make a ton of offseason adds, in order to improve in 2026, they’ll need several players to take the next step. The good news is there are plenty of candidates to have a breakout season this year.

Our 2026 Detroit Lions season predictions series continues today with our staff picks for 2026 Detroit Lions Breakout Player of the Year. And don’t forget you have the opportunity to cast your own vote at the bottom of the story.

Previously:

  • Offensive MVP predictions
  • Defensive MVP predictions

Who will be the Lions’ breakout player of the 2026 season?

Al Karsten: Tate Ratledge, Tyleik Williams

I’m going to keep it in the trenches, where the Lions’ first two draft choices of 2025, Tate Ratledge and Tyleik Williams, will transform their games by becoming more consistent overall while emerging as difference-makers on the interior of their respective sides of the ball. In the process, they’ll prove to be the next wave of young, homegrown pillars on this roster.

With both players approaching the idealized versions of themselves already in Year 2, they’ll also be complemented by a trio of breakout rookies turning heads in the trenches: Blake Miller, Derrick Moore, and Skyler Gill-Howard. All three should provide dynamic flashes alongside an above-average level of play throughout the season as they steamroll past minimal early-season rookie bumps in the road.

Together, that young group will help restore the identity of Dan Campbell’s gritty, tough, physical sons of guns—the type of team opponents don’t want to play because of the physical toll they’ll feel long after the final whistle.

Erik Schlitt: Tyleik Williams

The Lions’ defensive line showed a lot of improvement in training camp, and the play of second-year defensive lineman Tyleik Williams was a big part of that. Williams showed steady growth throughout his rookie season, but he looks like he’s capable of a huge sophomore jump in production this season.

John Whiticar: Tate Ratledge

There are a few returning players (Isaac Teslaa, Tyleik Williams) and a few rookies (Miller, Moore, Abney) that could stand out this year. However, I give the nod to Ratledge. I think this year, he could jump into the top-10 guards in the league and prove that he was not merely benefitting from playing next to Penei Sewell last season.

Ryan Mathews: DJ Wonnum

DJ Wonnum will be the Lions’ breakout player of 2026. Even though he just arrived in Detroit, Wonnum finds himself in one of the most coveted spots on a defensive line in the NFL, playing alongside Tyleik Williams, Alim McNeill, and Aidan Hutchinson.

Anthony Balaj: Sione Vaki

Vaki, the best pick of the 2024 draft class, earns a Pro Bowl nod as a special teamer, but also scores multiple offensive touchdowns.

Brandon Knapp: Isaac TeSlaa, Nick Whiteside

TeSlaa gets bumped up to the WR3 spot and with a rocky preseason, I think he can overcome those struggles and grow as a player. With LaPorta back, there should be less pressure from TeSlaa to excel, and less eyes focused on him. Defenses will overlook him still and I think he could have a solid contribution to the offense in 2026.

Whiteside starts the year on the practice squad, but I don’t think that stay is long-term. He had an excellent preseason and deserves to be on the 53-man roster, arguably as the team’s CB3. I believe Whiteside will be given chances to play and excel with the chances he’s given.

Morgan Cannon: Tyleik Williams

I am going with defensive tackle Tyleik Williams. In terms of statistical production, the rookie out of Ohio State didn’t make massive waves during his 2025 rookie year. Still, there were plenty of flashes for Williams. Especially when you turn on the all-22 and watch how he takes on double teams and is able to help the interior defensive line collapse the pocket around opposing quarterbacks. 

If fellow defensive tackle Alim McNeill can return to pre-injury form and Williams takes the next step or two in his development, the Lions’ defensive front could be fun to watch.

Jeremy Reisman: DJ Reed

I feel we were robbed of seeing what DJ Reed is truly capable of due to his early hamstring injury in 2025. Thus far in camp, it looks like he has his explosiveness back. Plus, with—hopefully—an improved pass rush, it can take some pressure off of Reed and force some errant throws. I wouldn’t be surprised if he tallied a few interceptions this year while remaining a strong presence in the run game.

item.title: NFL Kickoff Game preview: Patriots try to be more competitive in Super Bowl rematch vs. Seahawks
item.description: The Seahawks' encore to their Super Bowl season starts on Wednesday in Seattle.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL picking the New England Patriots as the opening game opponent for the Seattle Seahawks made sense, because it's a Super Bowl matchup.

It's also a little confusing, based on how that Super Bowl went.

For the most part we've had a run of competitive Super Bowls, but last postseason brought the second blowout in a row. The Patriots were overmatched from the start. The final score was 29-13 in favor of the Seahawks, but it was even more of a mismatch than the score would indicate. The Seahawks defense suffocated the Patriots, who didn't score in the first three quarters. The Seahawks led 29-7 before a meaningless touchdown by New England in the final three minutes. Seattle outclassed New England in every way.

That doesn't mean a rematch will go the same way, however. The Patriots got better at receiver, signing Romeo Doubs and then making a big trade for A.J. Brown. The many players still on the roster since last season will remember being embarrassed in the Super Bowl and want to make amends for it. Though, they will be without a key player as running back TreVeyon Henderson is out due to an ankle injury.

The Seahawks have some motivation too. They've been an overlooked champion this offseason as their NFC West rival Los Angeles Rams take up all the attention with their big roster moves. The Seahawks have had some losses this offseason, most notably running back Kenneth Walker III and offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak, but they were a dominant champion and won't take a backseat to the Rams.

"They made some big-time moves," Seahawks receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba said on ESPN, via Heavy.com. "I think them getting Aaron Donald is great for them and we understand that. But like I said, we kind of don't care. We're gonna take these challenges head-on and we're excited about it, looking forward to it, and really just worried about us and what we have to do."

Each team has plenty to play for in the opener, which was moved to Wednesday night to accommodate Thursday night's 49ers-Rams game in Australia. Hopefully this game is better than the last time the Patriots and Seahawks met.

Who needs it more?

The Seahawks have the benefit of being the Super Bowl champion. If they aren't as good this season it will be disappointing, but they earned a pass for at least a season. The Patriots didn't get that Super Bowl, and the offseason was surprisingly harsh for a 14-3 AFC champion. Everyone enjoyed pointing out how soft the Patriots schedule was and explaining how they'd regress. A win at Seattle to open the season would change that narrative instantly. A team with Drake Maye at quarterback and Mike Vrabel at head coach, surrounded by plenty of talent including an upgraded receiver room, shouldn't be going anywhere for a while.

Key player: Seahawks RB Jadarian Price

The Seahawks let Kenneth Walker III, the Super Bowl MVP, leave for the Chiefs in free agency. Part of the plan to replace him was drafting Price with the last pick of the first round. Many saw that pick as a reach, but Price is a talented player who happened to be behind Jeremiyah Love with Notre Dame. Zach Charbonnet is a capable back, but he's out at least the first four games of the season as he recovers from a torn ACL. That means a team that likes to run the ball is going to rely heavily on Price through September. He has the ability to become a big factor beyond that too, if he shows he can thrive in an expanded role while Charbonnet is out.

Betting market watch, by Ben Fawkes

The Super Bowl 60 rematch opened at Seahawks -3.5, but unlike the Super Bowl (which moved up to -5), the line has remained there and even ticked down to -3 at some books. Patriots CB Christian Gonzalez is no longer questionable with a contract dispute, as he'll suit up — while RB TreVeyon Henderson is out. Can Drake Maye look better against that Seattle defense? The Super Bowl champs haven't gotten much press this offseason, and they'll be waiting to take that out on New England on the field. The betting public likes Seattle to cover and I agree.

Check out more of Ben's work at the Yahoo Sports betting hub.

Fantasy football storylines, by Scott Pianowski

The Seahawks and Patriots kick off the 2026 season Wednesday night, a rematch of last year's non-competitive Super Bowl. Here are three fantasy angles to watch for:

1. Is A.J. Brown ready for a fresh act?

Brown has been a consistent fantasy star despite spending seven years on teams that ran the ball into the ground. Drake Maye enters Brown's life at a perfect time, but the Patriots understand that Brown will need maintenance — he's dealing with a chronic, degenerative knee condition. Brown always made sense as a second-round fantasy pick this summer, but we also have some floor concerns.

2. Will Jadarian Price hit the ground running?

The Seahawks sure hope so, with Kenneth Walker gone and Zach Charbonnet unavailable for several weeks. Price might have been a slight reach as an NFL first-round pick, but he could approach 18-20 touches in the opener, given how ordinary the depth chart is behind him.

3. Have the Seahawks unlocked Rashid Shaheed?

Seattle acquired Shaheed in the middle of the 2025 season and he did very little after the trade — a meager 15-188-0 line for nine games. But the organization still believes in Shaheed, giving him a three-year, $51 million extension after the season. Although receivers can sometimes produce quickly after a midseason trade (see Jakobi Meyers last year), slow onboarding is probably more common. We're eager to see if Shaheed can be a useful fantasy depth piece for 2026.

The NFL’s first-ever regular-season game in Australia brings a heated NFC West rivalry to the iconic Melbourne Cricket Ground.

The Rams enter as 3.5-point favorites against the 49ers, with the total set at 48.5. Kickoff is scheduled for Thursday, Sept. 10 at 8:35 p.m. ET, which will be Friday, Sept. 11 at 10:35 a.m. local time. 

My 49ers vs. Rams predictions dig into the Shanahan vs. McVay rivalry and the travel situations for each team, along with some outlier stats.

Read on for my NFL picks for Week 1's Thursday Night Football game.

 TOP PICK
49ers vs Rams prediction: 49ers +3.5 

The Los Angeles Rams are loaded, but history suggests this spread is too high. Los Angeles is just 8-11 straight up in 19 meetings between Sean McVay and Kyle Shanahan, with only four of those wins coming by four or more points. 

The preparation gap could be equally important.

The San Francisco 49ers arrived in Melbourne nearly a week before kickoff, while Los Angeles plans to land roughly 24 hours before the game following a 15-hour flight. That late arrival could leave the Rams dealing with jet lag and limited time to adjust to the time-zone change. 

They've obviously each done their homework on this, and it's interesting that they've come up with dramatically different approaches. Based on my experience with traveling to different continents and the subsequent sluggishness that comes with it, I greatly prefer the 49ers' plan.

San Francisco also enters as the healthiest version of the team we've seen in some time, with Nick Bosa confirmed to play and George Kittle trending in the right direction. Rams defensive tackle Aaron Donald won't play Thursday.

Take the points with a 49ers team fully capable of winning outright.

49ers vs Rams combo

San Francisco has repeatedly kept this matchup close and enters with a significant acclimation advantage after spending nearly a full week in Melbourne. The hook could be crucial in another tight divisional battle.

Brock Purdy averaged 16.3 rushing yards across nine appearances last season, and topped 20 in four of his final five games, including the playoffs. Los Angeles’ ferocious pass rush should create scrambling opportunities and force him out of the pocket.

Christian McCaffrey produced 82 and 66 receiving yards in last season’s meetings, and has cleared 40 in four of his last five against the Rams. Los Angeles struggled to defend running backs in the passing game last season, creating a favorable matchup for McCaffrey.

Expert Week 1 NFL moneyline picks

Patriots vs. Seahawks: Seahawks (62%)

Seattle’s defense held New England to just 13 points in last year’s Super Bowl, and Cover 6 is the name of the game when it comes to disrupting Drake Maye’s rhythm, as seen by his god-awful postseason stats. 

It may take a while for new Seahawks OC Brian Fleury to hit a groove, but he won’t have to call a perfect game to take down New England.

If a Diana Russini-related piece drops on gameday, all the better for Seattle’s odds.

Check out our full Patriots vs. Seahawks predictions!

49ers vs. Rams: 49ers (36%)

Los Angeles may be the best team in the NFL on paper, but the last time we saw this much preseason hype surrounding a team, the 2011 Eagles flamed out and finished 8-8.

Kyle Shanahan has always played his buddy Sean McVay tough, and I can’t look past the eerily different travel schedules that the 49ers and Rams have opted for.

I’m siding with the club that’s been in Australia for a calendar week rather than the one flying in 24 hours before kickoff. 

Buccaneers vs. Bengals: Bengals (66%)

We all know how lethal a healthy Joe Burrow can be with Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins out wide, and finally, the cavalry is coming on defense.

After adding Dexter Lawrence, Boye Mafe, and Jonathan Allen this offseason, along with drafting edge rusher Cashius Howell, the Bengals’ front four will be bringing plenty of heat.

With Tampa bringing in a new OC and future Hall of Famer Mike Evans in the process, I like Cincy to come out firing. 

Saints vs. Lions:  Lions (75%)

For the record, the Saints are my pick to win the NFC South, but a Week 1 matchup in Detroit is a tough spot.

This is a make-or-break year for Dan Campbell, and the Lions’ loaded offense should have no problem one-upping a NOLA unit starting the season without both Alvin Kamara and Jordyn Tyson.

Jets vs. Titans: Jets (48%)

Cam Ward’s preseason struggles can’t go unnoticed, and the Jets had a solid offseason, bringing in veteran defensive talent like Minkah Fitzpatrick and Demario Davis while drafting pass rusher David Bailey.

With fellow draft picks Kenyon Sadiq Jr. and Omar Cooper Jr. set to carve out nice roles in the offense alongside Geno Smith and Garrett Wilson, give me the Jets to start 2026 on a high note.

Ravens vs. Colts: Colts (38%)

As a Colts fan, I’m going to savor the brief window of seeing Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward on the field together before the injury gods inevitably send one (or both) to IR.

The Ravens should be excellent under Jesse Minter in the long run, but losing All-Pro center Tyler Linderbaum could create some early hiccups for their offense.

Give me Indy to pull off the home upset at Lucas Oil Stadium. For the Shoe!

Falcons vs. Steelers: Steelers (63%)

Atlanta went full “28-3 mode” this offseason, losing both Jalon Walker and James Pearce Jr. to injury and suspension.

Add in a messy QB battle between Tua Tagovailoa and Michael Penix Jr., and the Falcons dominated my Twitter FYP for all the wrong reasons.

More continuity around Aaron Rodgers and the Steelers in Year 2 will give them a leg up at home.

Bears vs. Panthers: Bears (60%)

The Panthers came back down to earth in the second half of last season, going just 3-5 SU over their final eight games. Now, they enter Week 1 with an already banged-up offensive line.

Ben Johnson will be looking for Caleb Williams and the Bears to make an early statement in the NFC, and Chicago will do just that in Charlotte.

If you listen to Jared Verse in interviews, he’ll make you believe for a second that the Browns are a real threat.

As much as I admire the guy’s positivity, you’re only as good as your QB in the NFL in 2026.

Deshaun Watson as the starter? Really?

Looking to defend their AFC South crown, the Jags are set to benefit from some good old-fashioned heat and humidity in the Sunshine State.

Bills vs. Texans: Texans (50%)

While Buffalo picked up disgruntled WR D.J. Moore and essentially swapped out an over-the-hill Joey Bosa for a similarly aged Bradley Chubb, Houston completely upgraded its offensive line without losing any key pieces from last year’s elite defensive unit.

Houston has kept Josh Allen to fewer than 200 passing yards in each of his last two games against the Texans, and they prevailed in both. Expect more of the same in Week 1.

Dolphins vs. Raiders: Raiders (63%)

As risky as it may seem, I’d seriously consider playing Las Vegas in your Survivor Pool this week.

Klint Kubiak isn’t messing around when it comes to revamping the Raiders’ identity, while the Dolphins are fielding the worst roster in the entire league.

The Raiders won’t be a playoff team this year, but they’ll be much more competitive and prevail in the Black Hole on Sunday.

Packers vs. Vikings: Vikings (54%)

Under Kevin O’Connell’s tutelage, I’m bullish on Kyler Murray making early waves in the Comeback Player of the Year odds, especially with Green Bay’s defense set to be without Micah Parsons to begin the season.

Minnesota has won four of its last five home matchups against the Packers, while O’Connell is 3-1 straight-up in Week 1 as Vikings head coach.

SKOL!

Commanders vs. Eagles: Eagles (68%)

Washington’s offensive line is an unmitigated disaster, and at this point, the Eagles losing A.J. Brown feels more like an addition than a subtraction for the psyche of Jalen Hurts and the Philly offense.

The Eagles have beaten this Commanders team by double digits in two of their last three meetings, with the lone outlier coming in a meaningless Week 18 QB duel between Tanner McKee and Josh Johnson.

Philly secures the dub at the Linc. 

Cardinals vs. Chargers: Chargers (82%)

Jim Harbaugh takes care of business against bad teams, and Geoff Clark detailed that in his Cardinals vs. Chargers early leans:

“Since 2024, LAC is 12-2 straight-up and 11-3 against the spread vs. teams with a 40% winning rate or worse.”

Rookie running back Jeremiah Love should make Arizona entertaining, but beyond that, the Cardinals remain a mess on defense with Jacoby Brissett as their bridge QB. 

Cowboys vs. Giants: Cowboys (60%)

John Harbaugh’s cringey opening team-meeting speech, Cam Skattebo’s offseason antics, and the general circus surrounding the Giants have me fading Big Blue out of the gate.

There’s plenty of noise around this team and an abundance of talent at the skill positions, but losing DT Dexter Lawrence II is an underrated blow. Meanwhile, Dallas has quietly avoided the Jerry Jones-induced drama that has defined so much of their recent offseasons.

Dallas is 9-1 SU over its last 10 head-to-head matchups against the G-Men, and I like the Cowboys to stand tall on Sunday night.

Broncos vs. Chiefs: Broncos (44%)

Eric Bieniemy will likely take a conservative approach, leaning heavily on Kenneth Walker III and the Chiefs’ ground game as Patrick Mahomes works his way back into form.

The problem? Denver’s defense was one of the best in football against the run last season, ranking second overall while allowing just 91.1 rushing yards per game and 3.87 yards per carry.

On the other side, Denver’s offense has added another explosive weapon in Jaylen Waddle, giving Bo Nix a true WR1 and Sean Payton another weapon to scheme with.

The wrong team is favored on MNF.

The New England Patriots have more pass-catching options in 2026 with some big-name adds at receiver. But when the chips are down, QB Drake Maye is going to turn to old reliable.

Tight end Hunter Henry was second in targets last season and is one of the best zone-busting TEs in the NFL, rated No. 4 versus zone at PFF in 2025. 

He’ll face predominantly zone coverage from the Seattle Seahawks defense in Week 1 (Seattle was No. 2 in zone usage in 2025).

Even before his renaissance in Minnesota and championship run in Seattle, I was a believer in Sam Darnold. Toot toot.

I expect there to be some hiccups in the Seahawks’ playbook, given Klint Kubiak is gone and new OC Brian Fleury is calling the shots. Seattle’s rushing attack isn’t what it was, leaving Darnold to shoulder the load.

While the inflated totals on those props may be too much to tangle with, I still like Stevenson to score a touchdown in Week 1.

Welcome back to FLEX Finder. It's been a long offseason and I've been tasked with covering most of it. The good news for you is that I have developed some very strong priors, and the bad news for you is that I'm the sort of person who is ready to move off my priors the second the new information we're about to gather over the first month of the season goes wrong. That leaves (especially) Week 1 and Week 2 as high-variance games for these sorts of articles. Strap in, we're about to be really right, really wrong, or ideally a mix of both.

Rules for this weekly article:

1) I will not recommend quarterbacks — There are plenty of good ones. You’re on your own there.

2) I will not recommend any running back who costs more than $5,000, wideout who costs more than $4,500, or tight end that costs more than $4,000 in DraftKings’ DFS slate — This was an easy cutoff for what a FLEX really is.

3) I consider any player who garners over 50 yards or scores a victory for the column — anything more you get out of that, well, great for you. Let’s set expectations low because we are combing for outliers.

Braelon Allen, NYJ — $4,700 — Denny's hatred of his swole body aside, we need to be clear that once we go this low on running backs, we are buying into divvied backfields and we are going to be naturally hit-or-miss. That said, I do believe that Allen is good. I do believe he is going to get red zone carries, since he did plenty of that last year before he got hurt. The Titans traded out T'Vondre Sweat for John-Franklin Myers in a move I think will make harder for them to stuff the run. The Titans were 21st in run defense DVOA last year and I bet they can go lower this year, with a defense in which the only linebacker even the strongest NFL heads can name is nursing a concussion suffered in an accident before the game. Of all the backs that are under our imaginary criteria, I feel strongest about the odds of Allen scoring this week.

Mike Washington Jr., LV — $4,600 — Maybe Ashton Jeanty is playing, and maybe he isn't. Let me ask a question: Shouldn't Washington Jr. get plenty of playing time anyway as Jeanty works back from the ankle injury? Wouldn't it make sense to ease Jeanty in? And don't Klint Kubiak backfields always divvy up plenty of work anyway? Alright. So once I've established I believe these things, I then look at an opponent that turned over seven spots on the waiver wire in Week 1 and looks like this:

(Depth chart courtesy of Ourlads.)

There are two established NFL players here: Zach Sieler and Jordyn Brooks. I like Jacob Rodriguez a lot, but he's a rookie linebacker in game one of his NFL career. The Raiders paid Tyler Linderbaum to run the ball. I think they do that here.

George Holani, SEA — $4,600 — My main prior here is that the Seahawks will use Jadarian Price as their lead back until Zach Charbonnet is healthy, and that it will be a split backfield at that point. But the Seahawks beats have been loud that Holani will be involved on third down, and you're almost universally better off betting against rookie running backs early in their first season. Maybe Price handles 70 percent of the touches here, but I think a 60/40 split is approachable for Holani. And while DC Zach Kerr did yeoman's work down the stretch last year, the Patriots don't have a ton of defensive talent outside of the secondary. They couldn't stop the Seahawks run game in the Super Bowl. And Christian Barmore is banged up. I think Holani's range of probabilities aim quite a bit higher than this.

Chris Brooks/Kaleb Johnson, GB — $4,500 and $4,400 — Someone has to run the ball in Green Bay, and are we really going to trust MarShawn Lloyd to make it full a whole game unscathed? Brooks has the third-down role set. I don't know how quickly Johnson can get up to speed but I liked him quite a bit coming out of Iowa and think he could prove he got a raw deal in time. I don't feel quite as strongly about this as my other picks here — running back dries up quick — but I think Lloyd could be looking at less time in the backfield than you'd think.

▶ Wide receivers

Kayshon Boutte, HOU — $4,500 — The answer to "which of Houston's young wideouts outside of Nico Collins do you want?" dried up quickly. The answer was Jayden Higgins, but his ACL decided we don't get to live in that world. Jaylin Noel had a bumpy, injury-filled camp. Tank Dell is on the PUP list to start the season. That leaves Boutte and Dalton Schultz as potential No. 2 target options for the Texans heading into Jim Leonhard's first game as Bills defensive coordinator. Someone has to generate fantasy points in this passing game and I'll bet on the guy who can get there with one catch.

Pat Bryant, DEN — $4,200 — I like a lot about what the Chiefs did this offseason defensively, but with Trent McDuffie jettisoned to LA, we're living in a world where they're playing a 2025 third-round pick, the sixth overall pick in this year's draft, and legendary Titans bust L'Jarius Sneed as their three cornerbacks. None of that scares me. Bryant, by all accounts, was one of the main stars of Broncos training camp and I think we can trust him to be in the starting three-wide for an offense that will throw a lot. I think he takes a step forward this year and it starts here.

Adonai Mitchell, NYJ — $4,000 — Did you know that the Titans fixed their cornerback room this offseason? They signed Alontae Taylor and Cor'Dale Flott to big deals, which is something that would sound a lot better if it didn't make their No. 1 cornerback Alontae Taylor and their No. 2 cornerback Cor'Dale Flott. There was nothing there last year. I think the Jets' pass offense will be more theoretically good than actually good this year, but this is a matchup to push in my opinion. Mitchell has been the toast of Jets camp and I think he'll have plenty of air yards in this game; I can't tell you how they'll end up, but this is the upside we hunt for.

Devaughn Vele, DEN — $3,500 — With Jordyn Tyson derailed by injury, Vele opens up as the pretty clear No. 2 receiver in New Orleans as the only two other non-Chris Olave receivers to make the 53-man roster are Day 3 rookies. Vele took his time to get on the field last year after he was traded to New Orleans near last cuts, but had a month-long stretch from Thanksgiving to before Christmas where he averaged 6.5 targets a game and piled on 239 total yards before a season-ending injury. I think he's got a window to be a very interesting fantasy play this year and the Lions secondary is diminished on talent with Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph both not playing.

Ja'Kobi Lane, BAL — $3,100 — I don't understand this one at all, so it has to be the case that he'll wind up a dud. This is a player who got training camp blurbs like this from beat reporters: "The rookie third-round pick has put together one of the best camps ever by a Ravens rookie, delivering a highlight reel catch almost every day." The competition around him for targets is almost non-existent: Rashod Bateman was only theoretically on the field last year and now has off-field issues, Mark Andrews feels diminished and old. It's Zay Flowers and a big vacuum for Ben Johnson's offensive coordinator last year, Declan Doyle. I like Lane to step into that vacuum, and I get to pit him against a weak Colts defense in Week 1 too? I legitimately don't understand.

▶ Tight ends

Juwan Johnson, NO — $3,700 — The designated survivor of the Saints receiver room. "This will be the thing that ends Johnson's fantasy viability," I write as he somehow puts up another 6/75 line in Week 1 against anonymous non-Jack Campbell Lions coverage linebackers. (Did you know Devin White is there?)

Greg Dulcich, DEN — $3,500 — Someone has to score fantasy points for the Dolphins this year. The defense is just too terrible for them to run the ball all season. Look at that depth chart I posted above. It doesn't even get into the safety room. I think the Raiders are another defense to pick on, and Dulcich was someone who was putting up some low-key usable lines last year in between Darren Waller injuries. At some point I figure one of the rookie wideouts will evolve into the main play here, but Dulcich is who I'm starting with as the main target.

item.title: Eagles News: ESPN picks Philadelphia to return to the Super Bowl against the Chiefs
item.description: Philadelphia Eagles news and links for 9/9/26.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation!

ESPN’s Bill Barnwell is apparently big on the Birds this year. Losing another Super Bowl to the Chiefs by three points sure wouldn’t be fun. I do think it would be cool to see a rubber match between these two teams. Same goes for a potential Super Bowl matchup against the Patriots. Especially cool if the Eagles actually go out and win the game.

Predicting the 2026 NFL playoff field, plus Super Bowl pick – ESPN

On the NFC side, I’ll pick the Eagles. I really believe in their defense as potentially being the league’s most complete unit, with difference-makers at all three levels and one of the best defensive coaches in Vic Fangio. There’s understandable skepticism about the offense after the Eagles made coaching changes and moved on from legendary offensive line coach Jeff Stoutland, but when Lane Johnson has been on the field, the Eagles have been successful. The star right tackle should be in the lineup more often in 2026, and the Eagles will have more success running the ball than they did a year ago. They’re one of the few teams that can compete with the Rams along the line of scrimmage and hold up in coverage against their playmakers. […] That leaves us with a Super Bowl rubber match. And as you can probably guess, if I believed enough in the Chiefs to pick them to win the AFC, I’ll ride with them to gain a measure of revenge and beat the Eagles in Super Bowl LXI. The added rushing element with Walker will give the Eagles issues they didn’t face when these two teams met in Super Bowl LIX, when the Chiefs basically abandoned the run altogether after the Eagles took an early lead. Without the ability to pin their ears back and strictly go after Mahomes as a passer, the Eagles might not be quite as dominant on defense this time around. Jalen Hurts has been spectacular in the Super Bowl matchups against Mahomes, but his one fumble in Super Bowl LVII helped swing seven points back to the Chiefs in a 38-35 victory. This one wouldn’t be quite as high-scoring, but let’s say that the Chiefs let Kelce (and potentially other members of the organization) ride off into the sunset. My pick: Chiefs 27, Eagles 24.

Eagles Film Preview: Commanders could struggle to stop Philadelphia’s rushing attack – BGN

Overall, I still favor the Eagles. Washington is installing a complicated new defensive system with a number of new starters, while the Eagles have far more continuity within the roster even if the offensive structure has changed. The obvious concern is that Jones’ entire defensive philosophy is built around making quarterbacks and offensive lines second-guess what they are seeing. That is probably not ideal for an offense playing its first meaningful game under a new coordinator. However, Washington also has to execute all of that complexity, and I’m not convinced the defensive personnel is good enough right now.

Every NFL team ranked by their 2027 Super Bowl chances entering Week 1 – SB Nation

Tier 1: Super Bowl Contenders. Nobody in our top five should really surprise anyone. These are the teams that are the elite of the elite, the cream of the crop, the organizations that either have everything together they need to hoist the Lombardi Trophy, or have issues so minor they won’t play a major role in their success. These are the teams that would stun us if they missed the playoffs, or got eliminated early. The Rams speak for themselves in this tier. The big question comes at the back end with the Ravens, who perennially get ranked high because they should have all the tools to make it, but end up with a fatal flaw in the playoffs. This year we see new head coach Jesse Minter having the capability to get them over that hump. No. 1: Los Angeles Rams, No. 2: Seattle Seahawks, No. 3: Buffalo Bills, No. 4: Philadelphia Eagles, No. 5: Baltimore Ravens.

Season Predictions w/BLG | OTSP #157 – Eagles Pin-Pull Network

Shane and Jonny are joined by Brandon Lee Gowton from Bleeding Green Nation to make predictions for the Eagles’ season.

Know Your Enemy – Jayden Daniels – Iggles Blitz

Daniels having to open the season against a loaded Eagles defense isn’t ideal for Washington, especially behind a questionable OL. The one advantage is that the Eagles won’t have good game tape to study. Washington limited their playbook in the preseason. The Eagles faced the Lions offense last year so they know the basic system, but they don’t know about Blough as a play-caller or how the offense will look with Daniels running it. I think it is fair to say he’s just a tad different from Jared Goff.

Why Jalen Hurts will flourish in Sean Mannion’s offense – NBCSP

And I don’t see any reason Hurts won’t flourish in this system. For starters, he’s flourished in every system so I can’t come up with a reason this would be any different. But Mannion really seems to have tailored the offense to what Hurts likes to do within the heavy play-action, under-center tenets the scheme is built on. This is a system that is quarterback friendly because the QB doesn’t have to read the whole field, most passes are high-percentage low-risk throws and there’s a heavy emphasis on running the ball and disguising plays pre-snap to keep defenses off balance. If the offensive line can stay healthy – and so far so good – and Dontayvion Wicks, Hollywood Brown, Elijah Moore and Makai Lemon can help make up for the loss of good ol’ What’s His Name in New England, and Saquon Barkley can run the ball consistently and productively, there’s nothing that can hold this offense back. Will it take a few weeks before it all comes together? Probably. The starting offense hasn’t played one snap of real football with Mannion calling plays, and that’s a little scary. They’ll go into Sunday’s opener vs. Washington without a dry run. But ultimately, this season is going to end the same way as 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025. With the Eagles in the playoffs and Hurts as one of the biggest reasons why.

Why Eagles OC Sean Mannion’s ‘beautiful mind’ matters more than new scheme – The Athletic

The Eagles did not game plan specifically for preseason games, so his first time planning and sequencing the calls comes Sunday against the Washington Commanders. Early feedback on the operation was favorable. Quarterbacks appreciated how quickly they heard the play call. The call sheet appeared organized. Communication remained sound. Substitutions were clean. Mystery still exists. The scheme, which the Eagles consider a competitive advantage, will evolve as Mannion sees how it fits the personnel. But Mannion’s success will depend on more than the binder he put together. It hinges on how he puts those ideas to work. “As the year goes on,” Mailata said, “we get to display what’s in the beautiful mind of his.”

‘It’s his time:’ DeVonta Smith enters 2026 primed to prove the Eagles — and himself — right as the new WR1 – PHLY Eagles

Dating back to the spring, there has been palpable internal enthusiasm for what Smith can become in new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion’s scheme. The 27-year-old has yet to surpass the 100-catch mark in his career mostly spent as the “1B” to Brown’s “1A.” How productive can he be if he starts getting thrown the ball more often? According to TruMedia, Smith ranked 12th in target share last year at 24.4%, while Brown finished 10th at 26.1%. But what if that number were closer to the 30% mark Jaxon Smith-Njigba surpassed last season (35.8%) and Puka Nacua approached (28.5%) in similar schemes geared around a play-action passing game that funnels targets to versatile pass catchers. Those close to Smith believe he’s ready for that workload. Actually, those close to Smith know he’s been not so patiently waiting for this. “Smitty fools everybody with this quiet, chill demeanor,” Murphy said. “Inside, there’s the heart of a diva receiver banging in his chest saying, ‘I want the ball, every time.’ I think he’s got a maturity and a respect for the team, so he goes out there just lunchpail and does the job. Whatever they’re going to ask him, he’s going to be in a position to execute it and do it. But he’s not lacking one ounce of confidence. Whatever anyone says about his body, he feels he’s 6-foot-5, 280.” Eagles wide receiver coach Aaron Moorehead added, “I think he’s always seen himself as a [No.] 1. And I think in this building we’ve always seen him as a one. You just had another guy that was a one. So for him, I think that he feels like it’s just his time.”

Riq Woolen wants to show Eagles fans the real him – PhiladelphiaEagles.com

It’s not every day that you hear a player coming off a Super Bowl Championship say that they look forward to proving themselves – but that is just the type of player Riq Woolen is. Selected in the fifth round of the 2022 NFL Draft by the Seattle Seahawks, the former UTSA Roadrunner had a chip on his shoulder. Woolen exceeded all expectations as a late-round pick in his rookie year, co-leading the NFL in interceptions (6) and earning selection to the PFWA All-Rookie Team. After four productive years in Seattle that cumulated in a Super Bowl LX victory, Woolen signed with Philadelphia in free agency to play opposite first-team All-Pro Quinyon Mitchell. At the start of Training Camp, Woolen said he felt like the “new guy in class” entering a secondary with Mitchell and Cooper DeJean. While Woolen became more acclimated with his teammates as Training Camp progressed, joint practices against the Patriots in New England proved to be a turning point for the fifth-year cornerback. “When you are in somebody else’s territory, you have no choice but to grow closer,” Woolen said. “We are all in a hotel for a week straight. All the meetings are in the hotel, we are all going to practice. So, being able to keep spending time with each other, I felt like it made us closer.”

Merrill Reese wants to broadcast Eagles games ‘forever.’ His wife helps him stay sharp after 50 years. – Inquirer

Merrill Reese sat in his living room chair, awaiting the rapid-fire questions from his wife as she prepared the longtime Eagles broadcaster for another game. “Thirty-one,” said Cindy Reese, reading off an index card listing Cincinnati Bengals running backs. Reese — who begins his 50th season on Sunday as the voice of the Eagles — needed a moment to think. Cindy, who has a doctorate in education and spent 20 years teaching middle schoolers, quizzes him the night before each game on the opposing players. She reads him a number and he spits out a name. They repeat the numbers until he masters it, like a student preparing for a big test. “I can drill,” she said. “I know what to do.”

Packers sign RB Damon Bankston – Acme Packing Company

The Packers worked out former Eagles CB Ambry Thomas.

DB Ambry Thomas […] It’s possible that Green Bay is still looking for answers to practice squad bodies at quarterback, where they signed Kedon Slovis from the Arizona Cardinals, and tight end, where the team retained Drake Dabney, but it also makes a lot of sense that they’re keeping an eye on defensive backs, too. The team only has 11 total defensive backs available between the 53-man roster and the practice squad, barely enough to make a two-deep at the position once you include nickel defenders. Eventually, the Packers will probably want to add numbers somewhere on the team in the secondary.

Cowboys projected to have 52% chance of making the playoffs – Blogging The Boys

Question 1: What percentage chance would you give the Cowboys to make the playoffs this year? ESPN gives Dallas a 33.9% chance of winning the division, behind the Eagles who are at 46.3% chance. (Good luck Washington and New York). They have the Cowboys with a projected win total of 9.2 wins. We’ll round that off to 9-8 record. The Cowboys went 7-9-1 last year in a poor season. Only two more wins on the year feels somewhat low. Does it to you?

The Washington Commanders release Week 1 depth chart – Hogs Haven

There aren’t many surprises on the document, with some clarity provided at the cornerback spot. Mike Sainristil and Amik Roberson are listed as first-teamers, with Rasul Douglas and Fabian Moreau behind them. There isn’t a slot cornerback position listed, so we’re unsure of who would play inside within the sub packages. Odds seem great that Roberton or Sainristil would move into the slot and Douglas would play on the outside.

Darius Slayton cut is a gamble the NY Giants might regret – Big Blue View

John Harbaugh is running a meritocracy, and Darius Slayton’s play this summer did not warrant him being ahead of any other wide receiver on the New York Giants’ roster. That is the biggest reason Slayton is an ex-Giant today. Slayton missed the entire spring after double sports hernia surgery. He had a quiet summer, admitting not long ago that he still was not running at 100%, though he felt “pretty good.” Malik Nabers is the Giants’ No. 1 wide receiver. Malachi Fields, Odell Beckham Jr., and Darnell Mooney were all better than Slayton this summer. For that matter, practice squad receivers Braxton Berrios and Dalen Cambre were also better. Slayton was ticketed for the game-day inactive list when Sunday’s season-opening game against the Dallas Cowboys rolled around. None of that means that cutting Slayton isn’t a massive gamble by the Giants.

item.title: 2026 Chicago Bears Season Preview: The Hunter is now the Hunted
item.description: A new year brings new expectations. Following their NFC North title in 2025, the Bears are now the hunted. @AaronLemingNFL previews the season.
item.content:encoded:
For every professional sports team, the end goal is always the same: Win a championship. Although that didn’t happen for the Chicago Bears in 2025, last season was easy to call a dream come true in many ways. Time flies, and sometimes it’s easy to forget the past. For most fans, 2024 was a season they’d like to purge from their memories forever. While living through former head coach Matt Eberflus’s last season in Chicago wasn’t pleasant, it also reminded everyone to enjoy the good times while they last. 

That’s exactly what Ben Johnson provided this team last season: Hope. 

Eberflus became the first head coach in franchise history to be fired midseason. While that alone isn’t uncommon, his failures came at the cost of Caleb Williams’ development as a rookie. Johnson not only righted those wrongs, but he also instilled a new culture in the team and the city that should leave a lasting impression for years to come. Now comes the hard part: Maintaining that success. 

It’s been 20 years since the Bears experienced back-to-back playoff seasons. Johnson and his team broke multiple “curses” last year. Will this be the next? Despite a lack of “flash” this offseason, the organization is optimistic its core is in place and that last year’s experiences (both good and bad) will give the team more tools to complete the road to Super Bowl 60. With the season set to kick off this week, let’s dive into our yearly Chicago Bears season preview. 

Offseason Additions

Pre-Draft:

  • LB Devin Bush
  • S Coby Bryant
  • C Garrett Bradbury
  • DT Neville Gallimore

Others: WR Kalif Raymond, DB Cam Lewis, DT Kentavius Street, DT James Lynch, LB Jack Sanborn, and Xavier Woods.

For the first time since the start of the rebuild, general manager Ryan Poles and the team took a more conservative approach to the start of the acquisition period. Losing Drew Dalman to retirement forced a trade for Bradbury, but the primary focus was adding speed. Both Bush and Bryant provide that in the second and third levels of the defense, while Raymond gives Johnson a familiar face to rely on at receiver. Gallimore, Woods, and Lewis should provide quality depth at their respective positions. Oh, and Jack Sanborn is back for a Round 2 with his hometown team. There’s no doubt that this free agency period lacked flash. Now, fans must hope that the core they established last season is enough to take them to the next level in 2026. They’ll be starting the season without Bryant at safety, which is a tough pill to swallow for a team that was hoping he’d set the tone for the entire defense. 

Draft:

Trades: 

  1. No. 460 to Tennessee Titans for No. 69 and No. 144
  2. No. 129 & No. 144 to Carolina Panthers for No. 124 and No. #166
  3. No. 239 and No. 241 to Buffalo Bills for No. 213
  • 1st Round (#25) S Dillon Thieneman (Oregon)
  • 2nd Round (#57) C Logan Jones (Iowa)
  • 3rd Round (#69) TE Sam Rousch (Stanford)
  • 3rd Round (#89) WR Zavion Thomas (LSU)
  • 4th Round (#124) CB Malik Muhammad (Texas)
  • 5th Round (#166) LB Keyshaun Elliott (Arizona State)
  • 6th Round (#213) DT Jordan van den Berg (Georgia Tech)

Following a lackluster free agency period, the Bears set their sights on yet another impactful draft class. Thanks to the DJ Moore trade, they came into the draft with four picks over their first three rounds. Round 1 started with a pleasant surprise in Thieneman. It was clear that safety was a top need for them, and having a player projected to go 10 picks early still on the board at 25 was about as good as it gets. They followed up the Thieneman pick with a trio of names on Day 2 that included Jones and two surprises in Roush and Thomas. Not many could have expected them to go all offense on Day 2, especially with the value of some of those picks in question. Luckily, they followed up on Day 3 with a trio of defensive players that, at worst, should provide quality depth over the next few seasons. 

All in all, this wasn’t the same impactful class as we’ve seen (on paper) over the last few years, but that was expected considering how much lower in each round they picked. All in all, they added what should be multiple Year 1 contributors with the idea of developing them into bigger contributors down the line. Fans shouldn’t expect the same early impact from this class, but as the season goes on, most should settle into roles that have them contributing weekly. 

Retained Free Agents:

  • LB DeMarco Jackson
  • LT Braxton Jones
  • OL Theo Benedet
  • S Elijah Hicks

Others: QB Case Keenum, DE Daniel Hardy, and iOL Jordan McFadden.

The ongoing trend of Poles and his front office not retaining many of their impending free agents continued this offseason. Despite having multiple starters hit the market, the team retained just two projected starters, along with some key depth pieces. Jackson was a must-re-sign after a breakout season, and picking up Benedet’s ERFA tag was a no-brainer. Retaining Jones for another year was a mild surprise, but much needed with Ozzy Trapilo’s status for the season still up in the air. The team also decided to keep their quarterback room together for another season, which seems smart after how well things went in 2025. All in all, each move made sense, even if fans expected to see more players back from last year’s roster. 

Contract Extensions:

  • RT Darnell Wright 4 years, $116 million ($93 million guaranteed)

Barring any last-minute surprises, Wright enters the regular season as the only player to receive a long-term extension this offseason. Given the money and resources needed for Caleb Williams and his offensive weapons in the near future, it makes sense. Wright was well-deserving of his new contract, and now holds the highest guarantee of any offensive lineman in NFL history.

Offseason Subtractions

  • S Kevin Byard
  • WR DJ Moore (Traded)
  • C Drew Dalman (Retirement)
  • LB Tremaine Edmunds (Released)
  • S Jaquan Brisker
  • DT Gervon Dexter Sr. (Traded)

Others: CB Nahshon Wright, WR Olamide Zaccheaus, DB C.J. Gardner-Johnson, DT Andrew Billings, LS Scott Daly, DE Dominique Robinson, LB Amen Ogbongbemiga, iOL Ryan Bates, DE Joe Tryon-Shoyinka, S Jonathan Owens, DT Chris Williams, TE Durham Smythe, CB Nick McCloud, WR Devin Duvernay, RB Travis Homer, and iOL Ricky Stromberg.

Heading into the start of the new league year, many expected Byard to be retained on an affordable deal. Despite productive talks heading into the legal negotiation period, the Bears chose a different direction at both safety positions. Moore’s trade surprised some, but for those who watched his usage before Rome Odunze’s injury, it was clear Johnson never valued him as a top option in his offense. Edmunds was a no-brainer to release, considering his play and money owed. Wright and Gardner-Johnson were two unsung heroes of last season’s secondary, but both got bigger deals elsewhere. The rest of the names on this list were simply depth pieces or role players. While it would have been nice to retain more of last year’s “core,” this type of roster churn is expected for every team in the league each offseason. 

Reasons for Optimism

1. Year 2 of Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams should produce even more fireworks.

As expected, last year’s offense looked worlds better than anything we saw under Eberflus. In some ways, it was reminiscent of Nagy’s first year as the team’s head coach, but if the early returns continue to trend in the right direction, Johnson’s reputation as one of the best offensive minds in football will be cemented. The work the first-year head coach was able to do in 2025 shouldn’t be overlooked, especially following a slow start to the season. Getting the most out of a young quarterback was his most important task, but the way he rebuilt the offensive line and drastically reshaped the running game might have been equally impressive. 

Chicago went from having one of the worst offensive lines in football to one of the best. Although two of their projected starters won’t be in the lineup for 2026, there’s reason to believe that Johnson and offensive line coach Dan Roushar will find a way to keep continuity, while further building off last year’s unheard-of turnaround. Not only will the offensive line’s success impact the pass protection, but it will dictate how successful they can be running the football. 

Unlike the defense, the offense has notable continuity. Outside of Ozzy Trapilo, Drew Dalman, and DJ Moore, all of last year’s playoff starters will be returning. While the inclusion of Moore in this offense would have been nice, the one-two punch of Rome Odunze and Luther Burden III should flourish in this scheme. In addition, you’d be hard-pressed to find a better tight end duo than Colston Loveland and Cole Kmet. Depth behind the team’s top two receivers will need to be sorted out, but it’s clear with the additions of Kalif Raymond and Zavion Thomas that speed was a priority. 

Of course, none of this really matters without top-tier quarterback play. Williams’ first season under Johnson had its fair share of ups and downs, but his late-game heroics and big-play ability aren’t easy to teach. Consistency from down to down will be a point of emphasis early in the season, but Year 3 has been home to some of the bigger breakouts when looking at the NFL’s current elite quarterbacks. Williams holds the keys to the kingdom for this team, and there’s little reason to doubt him taking the next step to stardom in 2026. 

2. The experience from last year’s NFC North crown and playoff victory should serve this young team well this season and beyond.

Even if the Bears aren’t outwardly young at any position on the roster, their core players sure are. General manager Ryan Poles and his front office did a nice job last offseason of finding the right mix of veterans to go with a younger foundation of players. Now that the needle has been threaded and their core has last year’s experiences under their belts, it’s fair to expect that it will serve them well with a tougher schedule and a bigger national spotlight on them. 

No NFL roster stays the same every year, and the Bears did lose some quality veterans who played key roles in last year’s success. Among those are: Kevin Byard, C.J. Gardner-Johnson, Tremaine Edmunds, Dalman, and Moore. That said, they added a Super Bowl-winning safety in Bryant and focused more on scheme fits than continuing to fit square pegs into round holes. Between last year’s success and the more experienced veterans added in free agency, fans should feel comfortable with the level of leadership on the current roster. 

More than anything, the experience gained by players like Williams, Loveland, Odunze, and Burden should give them confidence and a roadmap for navigating another 17-game season and beyond. It’s also worth noting that despite plenty of outside interest, the coaching staff remains largely intact for Johnson. All in all, the most important players on this roster are in place, and the experience gained from last year’s miraculous season should serve as a reason for the team and fans to believe they can do it again. 

3. Despite a mellow offseason in Chicago, the rest of the NFC North didn’t do much either. 

Following your favorite team’s offseason can be an emotional rollercoaster, as Bears fans are very familiar with at this juncture. Whether tearing down or rebuilding the roster from the studs, Poles has made plenty of headlines since taking over in 2022. Couple that with a different outcome against the Rams, and this offseason felt like one that could get the team over the top. Instead, Poles and his front office took a more conservative approach, leaving some fans to wonder whether or not they did enough to take the next step. 

While it’s not hard to argue that Chicago should have done more coming off such a successful season, sometimes it’s easy to ignore what goes on with the other three teams in the division.

 On paper, the Lions probably did the “most” of any team in the NFC North, but even then, there wasn’t a “splash” move that an objective observer would label as “groundbreaking”. Instead, they focused on the trenches, hoping their current core of players would stay healthier for the upcoming season. The Vikings had more losses than gains, although it’s worth noting that the Kyler Murray signing could be the most impactful move any team made. That said, they lost plenty of firepower on their defensive line, and still have other questions plaguing their roster. Finally, we get to the Packers. Losing defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley is going to hurt, but their lack of activity along the defensive line is what I’d be most concerned about as a Green Bay fan. With Micah Parsons expected to miss the first six (or so) weeks of the season, they’ll be relying on Lukas Van Ness and multiple unproven edge rushers to pick up the slack of the pass rush. 

Without getting too much into the weeds of what each team did (check out my 2026 NFC North Season Preview for that), it’s clear that the Bears were far from the only team in the division that feels like they can contend without breaking the bank or trading away high-round draft capital. Each year produces different results, but it’s key to take in all offseason context, and at least on paper, the Bears didn’t really lose any ground in the talent department within the division. 

Where They Stand in the NFC North

Last year, the NFC North was the only division in football to have all four teams finish above .500. Suffice it to say. However, even if the Detroit Lions and Minnesota Vikings took a step back and were labeled “disappointments” in 2025, the NFC North still had plenty of competition. Considering none of their four teams really did much to separate themselves on paper this offseason, it stands to reason that this should be another tightly contested race for 2026. 

Looking at the trend of betting odds, the Bears are a popular choice to finish outside of the top spot. In fact, there isn’t a single sportsbook out there (that I have found) that has the Bears as division favorites, despite their success last year. 

In some ways, it’s understandable. The Lions, who are the odds-on favorite, haven’t had a losing record in four seasons and have strung together a 27-7 regular-season record between 2023 and 2024. Despite their recent lack of postseason success, the Green Bay Packers have made the playoffs in six of their last seven seasons. Heck, even the Vikings have posted three winning campaigns over the last four years. In most folks’ eyes, the Bears must prove that they weren’t a fluke and have enough talent to sustain the wave of regression in one-score games. 

So, where does that leave Chicago in 2026? If there’s one lesson the NFL teaches yearly, it’s that parity is king. New playoff teams emerge every season, and there’s a case to be made for all four teams within the division. In addition, history is not on the Bears’ side. 2026 will mark 20 years since they’ve made back-to-back playoff appearances. For additional context, they’ve done it just twice since 1990. Even if fans don’t see the skepticism as warranted, there’s plenty of history to at least give the benefit of the doubt. 

Assuming good health, the offense should take another step forward in Year 2 of the Johnson-Williams pairing. The bigger question will be the defense and whether they did enough to truly improve their unit to compete for a Super Bowl. The team’s head coach said it best after their Divisional Round loss to the Rams, but it bears repeating: Momentum does not carry from season to season. Despite last year’s success, the Bears must go through the process again to succeed. The biggest change is that now they’ll be the hunted and won’t catch anybody off guard. 

The blueprint for another successful season is there, but the schedule is projected to be more difficult, and the NFC North might be the most competitive division in football. If they want to repeat as division champs and contend for a Super Bowl in 2026, Williams must take the next step, and the defense needs to improve significantly. Now, all that’s left to do is watch it play out.

Projected Record and Final Thoughts

On paper, the Bears will enter the 2026 season with one of the league’s hardest projected schedules. Sounds familiar, doesn’t it? We said the same thing last year, and as we saw over time, it didn’t pan out that way. That’s why fans should always be cautious with projecting seasons based on past years’ results. That said, the road back to a division title and the playoffs should be tougher. The Bears went from the hunter to the hunted, so it’s only natural that teams are going to approach them differently in 2026. 

Despite what projects to be a tougher schedule and the “surprise factor” being gone, this is still a very good team capable of matching or surpassing last year’s record. Getting off to a strong start will be key, and although there aren’t many lulls in the schedule overall, there aren’t many stretches on paper that feel too difficult to overcome. Without further ado, let’s jump into my 2026 season predictions.
