item.title: Lions scouting report: Saints a possible sleeper?
item.description: Diving into the New Orleans Saints heading into their Week 1 game against the Detroit Lions.
item.content:encoded:
In what was the longest offseason since the end of the 2022 season, your Detroit Lions are back to playing meaningful football! Training camp and preseason are over, the rosters are finalized (for the most part), and the regular season has arrived.

The Lions kick off at home in Ford Field to play the New Orleans Saints on Sunday in Week 1. The Saints are aiming to snag the NFC South divisional crown for the first time since 2020 and have higher expectations than last season. While most don’t believe this team can win it all, some think they can compete in what is known as the NFL’s easiest division. They have a young roster, but also veterans who can help them improve on last year.

An up-and-coming team like the Saints could make a statement with a win on the road against the Lions. Detroit, on the other hand, could use a win to start the season after how 2025 went for them. Let’s dive in on the Saints and how much they’ve improved ahead of Week 1.

New Orleans Saints

2025 Season

  • 6-11 record (4th in NFC South)
  • 28th in points for, 16th in point allowed
  • Overall DVOA: 28 (27th on offense, 13th on defense)

2025 was a slight improvement for the Saints over their 2024 campaign, with one more win. Expectations were low heading into last year, with question marks at quarterback and a new head coach in Kellen Moore. With a young roster, it was going to be a difficult season, but in the end, they came away with clearer answers and a vision for the future.

At quarterback, former starter Derrick Carr retired in May 2025 for health reasons, leaving the Saints with 2024 fifth-round pick Spencer Rattler and 2025 second-round pick Tyler Shough to battle for the starting job. Rattler won the job, but not for the entire season. After going 1-7, he was benched and replaced by Shough, who finished the year with 2,384 yards, 10 touchdowns, and six interceptions—and a 5-4 record. Shough also found the end zone three times on the ground for 186 yards.

The biggest issue for the Saints offensively, despite the early quarterback play, was the rushing attack. Starting running back Alvin Kamara finished last year with 471 yards and one touchdown (career lows), missing six games due to an MCL sprain, and the depth behind him was nowhere to be found. Devin Neal had 206 yards and two touchdowns, with other running backs like Audric Estime and Kendre Miller getting a combined 391 yards and two touchdowns. The leading scorer on the ground was Shough, which says a lot about the running back room.

When it came to passing the ball, the Saints found a lot more success, especially with wide receiver Chris Olave, who had the best season of his career. Olave finished with 100 catches for 1,163 yards and nine touchdowns. Another contributor was Rashid Shaheed, who had 499 yards and two touchdowns, but he was traded to the Seattle Seahawks midseason. Tight end Juwan Johnson had a career season as well, finishing with 889 yards and three touchdowns on 77 catches.

On defense, the defensive line shone brightest. EDGE Cameron Jordan led the team in sacks with 10.5 and forced two fumbles, but right behind him was EDGE Chase Young, who had 10 sacks and also forced two fumbles. The secondary was led by second-year cornerback Kool-Aid McKinstry, who paced the team with three interceptions and 17 pass deflections. The Saints’ run defense is what held them in a few games, allowing just 4.0 yards per carry, which ranked seventh in the NFL.

2026 offseason

Key additions: G David Edwards, RB Travis Etienne, RB Ty Chandler, LB Kaden Elliss, TE Noah Fant, EDGE Tyree Wilson (trade), K Daniel Carlson

Key losses: CB Alontae Taylor, LB Demario Davis, TE Foster Moreau

2026 NFL Draft picks

Round 1: WR Jordyn Tyson
Round 2: DT Christen Miller
Round 3: TE Oscar Delp
Round 4: G Jeremiah Wright
Round 4: WR Bryce Lance
Round 5: S Lorenzo Styles Jr.
Round 6: WR Barion Brown
Round 7: CB TJ Hall

Overall, the Saints have more talent coming in than leaving, a good sign that this team is headed in the right direction. Their biggest free-agent move was keeping Jordan around after he tested free agency for his final season. When it comes to new incoming talent, though, the biggest add was guard David Edwards. This should help both the pass and the run, with a veteran guard strengthening the front. The team also made a trade for Las Vegas Raiders EDGE Tyree Wilson, giving up a 2026 fifth-round pick to acquire him and a 2026 seventh-round pick, giving them a potential suitor to replace Jordan after he retires.

Running back Travis Etienne should see ample playing time with Kamara currently dealing with an MCL sprain. Linebacker Kaden Elliss gives them a younger linebacker core as Demario Davis left. Another replacement is tight end Noah Fant, who takes the spot of Foster Moreau and gives the Saints another viable threat in the passing game. The addition of kicker Daniel Carlson gives the Saints a big upgrade at the position, as their previous kickers, Blake Grupe and Charlie Smith, combined for a 71 percent field goal percentage. The biggest loss, though, was cornerback Alonte Taylor, and the secondary could be tested early, with few moves to bolster it.

The rookie class did add some much-needed depth. Getting three wide receivers, led by first-round pick Jordyn Tyson out of Arizona State. Tyson will miss at least the first four games of the season after being placed on IR with a hamstring injury. The Saints also got help on the interior defensive line with defensive tackle Christen Miller, and more depth at tight end with Oscar Delp. The offensive line has a potential future starter in guard Jeremiah Wright, and the secondary got a few late-round picks in safety Lorenzo Styles Jr. and cornerback TJ Hall.

2026 season outlook

New Orleans has a bit higher expectations in 2026. They are still an underdog to win the NFC South (second in odds behind the Buccaneers), but this could be a year for them to finally be on top again. They have their quarterback in Shough, and he’s been given some upgraded weapons—though his biggest one is on the sidelines for the moment in Tyson. The team must improve its running game, and it made moves to address that, but with Kamara already dealing with an injury, the depth might be tested sooner than expected.

On defense, it should be a slight improvement as the team got younger on that side of the ball, but lost key starters in Taylor and Davis. If the young guys can show out and fill the roles of the vets who came before them, there should be ample improvement. Moore will now be in his second year as a head coach, and that should give him a leg up on the year before, when everything was new and different.

The NFC South is anybody’s game this season. The Carolina Panthers won the title last year at 8-9, and they aren’t the favorites to win the division again. The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are currently the favorites, but they still have questions at wide receiver and on defense. The Atlanta Falcons could be uncertain at quarterback and just signed their star running back, Bijan Robinson, to a new contract. No team in the division is standing out as a clear-cut favorite, which could be the perfect time for the Saints to swoop in and get back in the playoffs.

Injury notes

Key players ruled out: DT Bryan Bresee (IR), RB Ty Chandler (IR), WR Jordyn Tyson (IR)

Key players to monitor: RB Alvin Kamara (MCL), EDGE Cameron Jordan (hamstring), LB Pete Werner (groin), CB Quincy Riley (groin)

Injuries have struck the Saints early this season at key spots. First, losing defensive tackle Bryan Bresee to a torn ACL back in July hurt the interior defensive line. Then losing Tyson for at least four games hurts the offense’s ability to move the ball through the air. Kamara isn’t likely to play Week 1, so expect Etienne to start at running back, and without Ty Chandler, the depth is questionable. Jordan could miss the game, but I expect him, along with Werner and Riley, to play.

Biggest strength: EDGE

Like last season, the edge defenders are this Saints team’s strength. If Jordan can play Week 1, he and Young will have some chances to get to Goff against Detroit’s retooled offensive line. While Lions left tackle Penei Sewell will hold up his end, rookie right tackle Blake Miller will likely go through some expected ups and downs. The Saints have some depth at the position in Carl Granderson and Wilson. Granderson got six sacks last season and was a part of the rotation to help the Saints edge position stay strong.

The trade for Wilson gives the Saints a chance to mold him and resurrect his career. Being a former first-round pick, Wilson has a ton of raw talent. However, he only has 12.0 sacks in 50 game appearances and seven starts. That said, he’s a depth player on this roster, which goes to show how deep they are.

Biggest weakness: Wide receiver/running back depth

Much like the Lions, the Saints have four wide receivers on their 53-man roster, but the difference is who they have there. While the Lions have Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, and Isaac TeSlaa as their top three, the Saints have two Day 3 rookies amongst their four (Lance, Brown). Chances are they’ll have to rely heavily on Olave and the tight ends to help provide more depth in the passing game until Tyson returns from his injury.

At running back, the team may be without Kamara and Chandler, leaving Etienne as the starter and Miller and Estime as the backups. The Lions are in a similar spot, so both teams face the same issue this week.

When a team lacks firepower at key positions on offense, it usually leads to lackluster performances. The Saints can still win the division if they play their cards right, but early on in the season, it’s going to be an uphill battle for the offense.

Key matchup: Lions offensive line vs. Saints defensive line

Detroit’s offensive line was one of the biggest factors in their 2025 failures. The opening game against the Green Bay Packers saw a lot of struggles, and the Saints defensive line could repeat that opening-week PTSD. With a backup center in Juice Scruggs starting, the entire five haven’t had as much time as they’d like to gel and build chemistry.

The Saints defensive line is a good first test for the Lions’ revamped offensive line. The EDGE rushers in Young and Cameron will be a tough battle for Lions rookie right tackle Blake Miller. The interior, while not as talented, should still give left guard Christian Mahogany (or Ben Bartch) and Scruggs enough work to handle. If the Lions can hold back this Saints defensive line, it could be a blowout. If the Saints defensive line can slow down Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs or get pressure on quarterback Jared Goff, there’s a chance for an upset at Ford Field come Sunday.

Vegas line for Sunday: Lions favored by 6.5

item.title: Steelers’ secondary concerns and other storylines to follow in Week 1 vs. Falcons
item.description: Steelers Read & React breaks down what to watch for in the season opener vs. Atlanta.
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 NFL season is on the horizon. And after weeks of discussions, predictions and analysis, we’ll finally get to see some of the year’s biggest Steelers stories thus far finally play out on the football field as Pittsburgh hosts the Atlanta Falcons on Sunday.

With that in mind, here are some of the biggest narratives Read & React will be monitoring this weekend:

How will the new-look secondary perform?

RB: There is a lot we still don’t know about the 2026 Pittsburgh Steelers, but the secondary might be where the most uncertainty lies. When I predicted which Steelers units would be most likely to finish in the NFL’s top 10 in the upcoming season, the pass defense was the hardest to get a read on.

With a cornerback room made up of Joey Porter Jr., Jalen Ramsey, Jamel Dean, Asante Samuel Jr., Brandin Echols and Daylen Everette, there’s a legitimate argument that this group could be elite. But at the same time, it isn’t difficult to imagine scenarios that result in the Steelers dropping closer to their 29th-in-the-NFL ranking in passing yards allowed per game in 2025.

There’s a lot that can go wrong, especially early in the season.

Starting with Porter, who is expected to be the top name in the secondary this year, there’s a chance he doesn’t even play if he doesn’t receive an extension by kickoff. But assuming he does suit up, it’s worth noting Porter missed the bulk of summer on the Physically Unable to Perform list with a reported back injury, and never took a rep in the preseason as a result. Rust could be a factor early-on in his game.

Most of my concern regards the safety room, however, which will be especially undermanned early in the season with starter DeShon Elliott opening the year on injured reserve. Veteran Rayshawn Jenkins is expected to start alongside Jaquan Brisker, but I’d expect a short leash and Ramsey to rotate in at safety as well sometimes to give the group some needed extra range.

We haven’t seen much of free agent signing Jamel Dean this offseason, who has flown under the radar a bit this offseason despite having the makings of a high-end CB2. He wasn’t far behind Porter in most metrics in 2025, allowing a 63.1 passer rating when targeted and a 49.2% completion percentage for Tampa Bay.

Dean will turn 30 this season, meaning age is a concern but a Darius Slay-esque drop off in play isn’t expected this season. However, Dean’s availability is a minor question; he’s averaged four missed games per season in the last three years.

But the arguable biggest piece of the puzzle is how that assortment of names will mesh with the scheme of new coordinator Patrick Graham.

Graham is seen as a highly-adaptable defensive mind, but if the looks he did show in the preseason are any indicator, he isn’t afraid to use a number of coverage concepts in one game — or blitz. Graham sent a heavy dose of pressures in Pittsburgh’s slate of August games, putting the team’s secondary (that was missing names such as Porter, Ramsey and Brisker, to be fair) in tough spots where they didn’t always succeed.

Now up to almost-full strength, we’ll get to see how Pittsburgh’s defensive backs mesh with Graham’s coaching in a real game. It’ll also be interesting to see how Porter’s speciality in press-man coverage fits into a more diverse scheme.

The good news is that while the Falcons boast a talented group of offensive weapons, starting quarterback Tua Tagovailoa shouldn’t present a massive challenge for the defense in Week 1. But if things go poorly against Tagovailoa, who was benched by the Dolphins late last year, it could be time to worry a little bit.

How soon can top rookies make an impact?

RP: As Week 1 gets closer, the team is letting out more info about how head coach Mike McCarthey sees the roster at this early stage of the season. The team has put out its first depth chart of the season Tuesday, which came with some items to ponder. While it’s wise to remember a depth chart is ultimately just a list of names that a coaching staff can quickly pivot from on game day, it is also useful for setting initial expectations.

It isn’t shocking that the Steelers top two rookies, first-round selection Max Iheanachor and second-rounder Germie Bernard, are absent from the list of starters. McCarthy and the Steelers’ brass have been telegraphing that for most of August, even with the two youngsters giving plenty of reason for optimism this summer. But how long can we expect either rookie to remain sidelined?

We’ll start with Iheanachor, the team’s top pick. The Arizona State product was the talk of Steelers camp in the early days of training camp, and might have had a legitimate shot to start in Week 1 if he hadn’t suffered an untimely shoulder injury that sidelined him through the first two preseason games. With that amount of time missed, it was going to be next to impossible for him to earn a starting spot with a viable alternative at the Steelers disposal. The Steelers believe Dylan Cook is just that.

“We feel really good about Dylan,” McCarthy told the media Monday, when he said that Cook was taking most of the reps at right tackle this week.

I think it’s safe to pencil Cook in as the starter for Week 1, but I also think McCarthy’s comments are telling. Cook was taking the majority of the snaps, but not all. McCarthy also declined to outright name Cook the starter when he was asked. This, paired with other comments from the head coach, as well as from the team’s offensive coordinator Brian Angelichio, should make it clear that Iheanachor taking over this season is a matter of when and not if, as long as health allows.

Projecting when Iheanachor might take over is trickier. He was healthy enough to play in the final preseason game, so I have to believe he is physically capable of going now. You wouldn’t want to see it go down this way, but like most NFL backups, he’s realistically just one injury away from entering the lineup. But barring that, I’m eyeing Week 5 and October 11 as a possible entry date. That would give him another month to ramp up, and the Colts have one of the least intimidating pass rushes in the NFL. If they feel like that start date is still too soon, then perhaps coming out of their bye week against the Bengals in Week 10 might be another alternative.

McCarthy wasn’t just playing coy about the right tackle position, though. Instead, he said he wouldn’t discuss the starters, citing it as an attempt to keep the Falcons off balance heading into the matchup. While I ultimately don’t believe that will have much impact on the game one way or the other, it’s a long-held tactic by many football coaches I’ve met across all levels of football, so it shouldn’t be that surprising.

But unlike Iheanachor, I’m having a hard time believing the Steelers will keep Bernard sidelined for long. For one thing, Roman Wilson barely has any more on-field NFL experience than the rookie entering his third pro season. For another, Wilson was generating camp buzz last summer too, but until we see it translate to production in games, I think it’s fair to remain skeptical. And some recent comments by Aaron Rodgers really stood out to me when we consider the performances we saw both these receivers give in the preseason. After praising Bernard for not repeating mistakes, the Steelers QB was about Roman Wilson and had this to say:

Rodgers is famously hard on his receivers. Rodgers’ displeasure with former Steeler Mike Williams was something he voiced to the media when both men were on the Jets, and certainly played a part in Williams becoming available to Pittsburgh that season. Wilson was also reportedly a player Rodgers was frustrated with in 2025. Perhaps Rodgers is just encouraging Wilson in his own way, but I think Wilson’s role on the team has a far more limited path, regardless. Wilson is a player who really needs to play in the slot to succeed, and Bernard is simply a far more versatile piece in the offense who can play all three receiver positions.

I don’t want to overhype a preseason performance that accounted for just 48 passing snaps, but Bernard made quite the impact in his limited playing time. He drew eight targets, which equates to a target share of roughly 17 percent. For comparison, DK Metcalf led the team in target share in 2025 with 19.5%. Bernard turned those targets into five receptions for 64 yards (12.8 Y/REC) and a score. He created 46 yards after the catch, forced nearly as many missed tackles (4) as receptions, and did so with an average depth of target (ADOT) of just 7.0 yards.

That last stat is the one I found most appealing to this particular version of Rodgers, whose ADOT in 2025 was just 6.4 yards. Rodgers is looking to get the ball out quickly and avoid hits. If that number stays low — and it should, as Rodgers has a career ADOT of 8.5 and hasn’t posted a figure above 9.0 yards since 2019 — his receivers are going to have to shoulder a lot of the burden when it comes to creating explosive plays. That fits Bernard’s skillset far more than Wilson’s. Wilson, a one-year starter in college, forced just nine missed tackles during his time in school and generated 576 career YAC, with 221 YAC as his highmark in his final year at Michigan. Bernard, meanwhile, had 28 missed tackles forced during his two years as a starter at Alabama, and totaled 993 YAC with a single-season high of 394.

If Bernard can demonstrate an ability to make plays like this during the regular season, it won’t be long until he overtakes Wilson in weekly snaps.

Other storylines to watch

  • This week, Mike McCarthy said the Steelers’ offense is built around Aaron Rodgers this year. While the Pittsburgh passing offense showed off some new concepts in the preseason, including a heavier emphasis on intermediate middle-of-the-field passing, will it look more like last year’s Steelers once Rodgers is the quarterback under center? — RB
  • What will the pass rush rotation look like? The Steelers’ initial depth chart listed three outside linebackers as starters — TJ Watt, Alex Highsmith, and Nick Herbig — with just one safety as a starter. Does this mean the team will be playing all three pass rushers at the same time more often than we expect? I’m skeptical the team plans to do that too often, as that would likely necessitate them playing a one-high safety deep, and their safeties are all better suited near the line of scrimmage. The team might try to get all three edge players on the field occasionally with creative looks, but I suspect that will more often than not involve swapping out one of the inside linebackers rather than a member of the secondary. I’d wager this implies a more frequent rotation of the top three than we’re used to, with Jack Sawyer mixing in as well. Definitely something to monitor against the Falcons. — RP
  • Is a Year 3 leap from Payton Wilson on the way? He showed promise as a rookie but seemingly failed to take a step forward last year, even losing playing time late in the season to Malik Harrison. Patrick Graham has helped boost the careers of middle linebackers in the past, and a bigger role from Wilson in 2026 would bode well for one of the defense’s weaker position groups, as well as Wilson’s future as a starter. — RB
  • Will we get a clearer picture of how the Steelers plan to deploy their running back duo of Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle? Will the two be trading drives? Or will they have more specific roles, such as Dowdle gaining a goal-line and short-yardage role, and Warren playing more third downs? I think either approach could work, but the latter option could cause us to see more of one back than the other depending on game scripts. — RP
  • The Steelers are clearly expecting big things from Keeanu Benton after a four-year, $72 million contract this offseason, and Derrick Harmon will also need to further establish himself as a long-term piece after being selected in the first round last year. With Cam Heyward closing out his career in the near future, Pittsburgh needs some of its younger defensive line talent to step up. 2025 fifth-rounder Yahya Black could be part of that equation as well. A good sign against the Falcons would actually be the Steelers giving Heyward more snaps off, signifying a higher level of confidence in the younger talent. — RB
  • Special teams. The Steelers will have a lot to monitor in this oft-forgotten facet of the game. Punter Cameron Johnston is back with the Steelers, and has been placed on injured reserve in each of the past three seasons, including his last stint with the Steelers in 2024. Rookie returner Kaden Wetjen is the listed starter at both returner positions. After showing some life in the last preseason game against the Bills, he’s looking to put a rough summer behind him. Wetjen can’t afford to have many fumbles or procedural miscues if he wants to stick through the whole season. It will also be interesting to see how the Steelers’ special teams play as a whole. PFF graded the Steelers as the second-worst special teams unit in the preseason, with only the Vikings graded lower. With the departure of several key players who played punt and kick coverage — Connor Heyward, James Pierre, Chuck Clark, Kenny Gainwell, Jabril Peppers, Malik Harrison, and Miles Killebrew — the Steelers have lost a combined 556 kick and punt coverage snaps from a year ago. There could be some early bumps and bruises while the Steelers try to figure out who can best fill those roles. — RP

item.title: Broncos at Chiefs preview: Denver aims for fast start
item.description: The Broncos will look to open the 2026 season with a big road win on Monday Night Football against Kansas City.
item.content:encoded:
The wait is over.

This is true on multiple levels. The Denver Broncos will open the season. And quarterback Bo Nix is set to return to the field after an ankle injury ended his and the Broncos’ season.

But there is something different about this season opener. Denver is coming off its best season in a decade, having hosted and played in the AFC Championship Game, claimed the No. 1 seed in the AFC, won the AFC West, and beaten Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills in one of the best wins in franchise history.

Now, can Nix and the Broncos build off that incredible season and take the next step to the Super Bowl? The first test comes on Monday Night Football against Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs.

FanDuel Sportsbook currently has Denver as the slight road underdog to its division rivals. The Broncos are +2.5-point underdogs to host Kansas City. The total sits at 43.5 points, with a lean toward the under at -112.

Offensive Rankings (2025) 

Denver: Tenth in total offense (352.1 yards per game), 18th in rushing offense (118.3 YPG), eighth in passing offense (233.9 YPG), 13th in scoring offense (24.1 points per game).

Kansas City: Thirteenth in total offense (342.9 yards per game), 22nd in rushing offense (109.7 YPG), ninth in passing offense (233.2 YPG), 20th in scoring offense (22.5 points per game).

Defensive Rankings (2025)  

Denver: Fourth in total defense (291.6 yards per game), second in rushing defense (90.2 YPG), 10th in passing defense (201.4 YPG), fifth in scoring defense (19.7 points per game).

Kansas City: Tenth in total defense (307.9 yards per game), ninth in rushing defense (103.4 YPG), 12th in passing defense (204.5 YPG), fourth in scoring defense (19.6 points per game).

Here are the MHR staff’s keys to Monday night’s game.

Start fast

This applies to Monday’s game and the season. One of the reasons Nix and the Broncos had so many comeback wins last season is that the offense started slow. The best way to ensure you don’t have so many come-from-behind, one-score wins in 2026 is to have the offense consistently start games faster. There’s no better time for that than Monday Night Football in Kansas City to open the season. And why not do so in Davis Webb’s first game as the offensive playcaller? Send a message to the rest of the NFL. On the first play from scrimmage, dial up a deep shot to Jaylen Waddle and test that Chiefs secondary. Coming away with an opening-drive touchdown on offense puts Denver in a great position to start the season with a big road win. — Ian St. Clair

Stop the run

Make the Chiefs one-dimensional. Force Patrick Mahomes to prove he can carry his team with a surgically repaired knee. — Adam Malnati

Close the deal on third downs

Whether on offense or defense, the Broncos will win if they beat the Chiefs on third down. — Tim Lynch

Score more points than KC

This will be a tough opening week matchup, but the key to the game remains the same. Score more points than the other team. According to advanced metrics, the Broncos are undefeated when they score more points than their opponents. So, if they do that on Monday Night, they will defeat their division rivals and start the year 1-0. — Scotty Payne

Win the turnover battle

Creating more turnovers has been a focal point of the team’s defense all season long. In order to win on the road at Arrowhead, the Broncos have to be on the right side with respect to turnover margin. Whether it’s a key interception, a strip sack, or a force fumble elsewhere, the Broncos’ defense has to make a few big plays to come out of Kansas City with a victory in Week 1. — Christopher Hart

Test Chiefs secondary

Push matchups hard against the Chiefs’ reconstructed secondary. That unit is debuting three new starters and trying to replace a whopping 2,415 defensive snaps vacated by McDuffie, Watson, & Cook. With 29-year-old L’Jarius Sneed bracketed by two young CBs, that secondary should present some big-play opportunities with the talent matchups the Broncos’ WR group and receiving RBs bring to the table. Let’s see Waddle & Sutton debut a Thomas & Sanders style lightning & thunder WR duo in strong fashion. — Taylor Kothe

Force second- & third-&-long

The Broncos defense allowed a league-best 4.0 yards per play on first down in 2025 and only 15% of first downs on first down — also league-best. They need to continue that against the Chiefs on Monday night. Get them off schedule and force them into second, third, and long counts. The Broncos need to take advantage of the weak KC offensive tackles and bring pressure with four, which will force Mahomes to make throws into tight windows, leading to incompletions and turnovers. — Joe Mahoney

What are your keys to Monday’s game?

item.title: Exactly how this Cardinals’ receiver group is shaping up
item.description: This new offense is going to throw the ball quite a bit
item.content:encoded:
The Arizona Cardinals are dotting their “i’s” and crossing all the “t’s” as they prepare to play their first game of the season this weekend against the Los Angeles Chargers.

This is an exciting time for both the coaching staff, the players, and the Cardinals fanbase.  

RELATED:CARDINALS EXTEND MICHAEL WILSON

This new offensive system is the headline of this year’s team.

New head coach Mike LaFleur has taken his experience under similar systems used with the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers. Does this mean that the Cardinals will have the offensive firepower of their division foes LA and SF?

Yes and no. Yes, it is designed similarly, with a lot of schemes, player personnel, and traits the same. No, in that this doesn’t happen overnight.

But this offense is loaded with talent. That is, on paper.

It all starts with the offensive line and the talent of the quarterback. We will see if both of these boxes become checked as games fall off the calendar.

The true test of the new offense is how the receiver room is utilized. Let’s do a deep dive.

“X” receiver

The X receiver lines up wide from the offensive line. Back in the day, it was referred to as the “split end.” This position is responsible for running a complete route tree, having good moves, physicality, and the ability to get downfield.

Marv Harrison (6’-3”, 220 pounds) is the Cardinals’ X receiver. It is what he played in college, and last year’s coaching staff – along with LaFleur’s guys – have kept him there. Harrison had a ton of success in the X at Ohio State, so why relocate him and attempt to teach him a new job?

Just imagine if Harrison can take a huge leap this year. Name a receiver award in college, and that hardware became a fireplace mantelpiece for his household.

There are plenty of questions regarding Harrison, and it all begins with his durability. He spent his entire career at all levels without ever having any major injuries, but last year he was in and out of the lineup. If he can remain upright, he can become a very valuable tool in this offense.

This position typically remains isolated all game. In LaFleur’s system, Harrison must be highly versatile and will be moved around from side to side quite a bit. This is because of tactical responsibilities. One of these is the ability to absorb and fight off physicality from the outside cornerback, who can jam Harrison as soon as the ball is snapped. His job has no cushion against aggressive press coverage, and he has to be able to beat a jam. The X has the ability to use the sideline to his benefit.

The X must be a good downfield blocker. Harrison is considered a willing and capable blocker, although this is not his strongest asset. While this offense will use quite a bit of 12 and 13 personnel, this will often leave the X isolated in man coverage for his number to be called, or simply running the decoy on a clear-out route for another receiver underneath.

The main job of the X is to win those isolated man matchups. Harrison showed in college that that is his style of play anyway.

“Z” receiver

This is where it gets interesting. Last year’s sensation in this offense, Michael Wilson (6’-2”, 213 pounds) is the Z receiver. This position is different from last year’s offensive scheme. Back in the day, this was referred to as the “flanker.”

Look at the Los Angeles Rams. The Z is Puka Nacua. Look at the Seattle Seahawks. Their Z is Cooper Kupp.

Typically, the Z receiver is the secondary option, but in LaFleur’s offense, it is the engine that sparks the passing game.

The Z is a step off the line of scrimmage as another outside receiver and is able to go in motion.

Part of the scheme for the Z is that it heavily utilizes play-action concepts that strike the intermediate portions of the field. This helps the offensive line because plays don’t take that long to develop, and the ball is out pretty quickly. Now, it does require a receiver who isn’t afraid to run crossing routes and deal with hard-hitting safeties.  

As the Z the past three seasons, Nacua had 160, 106, and 166 targets, and 1,486, 990, and 1,715 yards, respectively. And who was Nacua’s coach? LaFleur.

Slot receiver

This position sits inside its own little pocket outside of either side’s offensive tackle, or if a tight end is lined up. He must be a step off the line and have another receiver on his outside shoulder. He is another guy who will often go into motion and run the ball on the jet sweep. Usually, this is a smaller receiver.

For now, Kendrick Bourne (6’-1”, 205 pounds) is playing the slot.

Tyreek Hill is a great example who perfectly fills this role by getting up to speed before he turns upfield and has a good running start, often just blowing by his defender. And while Bourne isn’t running in the 4.3 range, his time in the 40 was 4.68, so he doesn’t have that flat-out speed, but he does have quickness.

This is a player who rarely gets jammed at the line and doesn’t have the sideline to work with or help him out with bad throws. Bourne is used to the short passing game, which is what the slot was invented for. All it takes is to fool just one defender, and either the center of the field or a soft zone towards the sideline is what he is working for. More than the other two positions, the slot guy must be able to create separation. And after he has gotten some space between himself and the defender, he must be able to defend himself against a head-hunting safety.

At times, Bourne will be asked to take it deep, usually in center field. By taking his routes down the middle of the field, he has the advantage of knowing which direction he will break off his route.  

The depth

There will be some four-receiver sets, but only once in a while. But this offense would rather stick another tight end on the field than four pass catchers. When it does happen, most likely you will see Simi Fehoko (6’-4”, 225 pounds), who is the backup to Wilson, as WR4.

Two players who should get some snaps are Jalen Brooks (6’-1”, 205 pounds) and the rookie, Reggie Virgil (6’-3”, 187 pounds). Devin Duvernay (5’-10”, 202 pounds) is also listed in the receiver room, but most likely he will be strictly a kickoff and punt returner.

Brooks is the guy who might be able to strip away some snaps from Bourne. He has an uncanny ability to get open in deep soft zones and is fearless about being around defenders. He will take hits and secure the catch extremely well.

The coaches are very high on the rookie Virgil. But just remember, it is a very deep room. And he is in his first year, so his best friend is patience.

This entire group for the past two years pretty much was reliant on the development of Harrison, who was taken with the fourth overall pick and was expected to become the next Jerry Rice and blow up the league.

But with the development of Wilson last year, and the experience of Bourne being signed away from the 49ers (who run this same offense) and the preseason success of both Brooks and Virgil, the Cardinals won’t have to rely on Harrison so much this year. If he continues to get injured, the offense is no longer decimated by his absence. There are guys now who can become plug-and-play, and the beat goes on.  

If Harrison can remain vertical, if Wilson can grow his game even further, and if Bourne can fill his role with his nine years of experience, this will give the Cardinals what they have been missing for many, many years since the glory days of Larry Fitzgerald.

A balanced passing attack.   

The Cardinals open Week 1 on Sunday, September 13, on the road against the Chargers. Kickoff is at 4:25 p.m.(Eastern) and will be broadcast on CBS.

item.title: NFL survivor pool picks, strategy: Week 1 safe, value, and trap options
item.description: NFL survivor pools are back as the NFL season gets going. David Fucillo provides tips in Week 1, offering up safe, value, and trap picks.
item.content:encoded:
It’s football time! The 2026 season is underway with Week 1 starting a day early. The Patriots and Seahawks kick things off on Wednesday this year because the 49ers and Rams are squaring off in Australia on Thursday. Due to the time difference, the NFL decided to kick this season off a day earlier than usual.

The start of the season means the return of Survivor pools. If you’ve never played before, a survivor pool involves picking one team each week that you think will win. If your team wins in Week 1, you can make a pick in Week 2. If your team wins in Week 2, you can make a pick in Week 3, and so on. The catch is that you cannot pick a team twice. You could very well use a heavy favorite in Week 1, but you won’t have access to them later in the year if you’re alive in the closing weeks. Most pools knock you out after one incorrect pick, but some do offer a double elimination process.

Whatever the case, there is plenty of strategy in determining which team you will take each week. SB Nation is here to help as we take a look at the safest choices, best value picks, and then trap picks. Normally this column will publish on Thursday, but with the early start to Week 1, we’re publishing a day early.

I’ve included odds for the favorite in each game, courtesy of FanDuel.

Safest picks

Chargers (-9.5) over Cardinals
Jaguars (-8.5) over Browns

The two biggest favorites are the safest you can use this week. The Cardinals and Browns will probably not go winless this season, but both are among the worst in the league in win totals. Meanwhile, the Chargers are fifth in Super Bowl odds at FanDuel while the Jaguars are in the middle of the pack, and both teams have second best odds to win their respective divisions. There’s no reason to get cute in Week 1, especially if you don’t have more than two entries in your contests.

Best value picks

Steelers (-3.5) over Falcons
Raiders (-3.5) over Dolphins

If you’re playing with only one or two entries, I think you go safe right out of the gate. But if you want to get a little cheeky, the Steelers and Raiders are intriguing. The Steelers win total sits at 8.5 with the under getting the juice, while the Raiders win total sits at 5.5 with the over getting the juice. The Falcons and Dolphins are both dealing with serious quarterback questions and low expectations. You might use the Steelers in Week 8 when they host the Browns, but you likely will not use the Raiders again this season barring something dramatic changing for them or one of their opponents. The value lies in not using them again.

Trap pick

Lions (-6.5) over Saints
Eagles (-5.5) over Commanders

The Saints are as big a question as there is this season. Tyler Shough raises all sorts of red flags, but if you’re onboard with him, you might be a fan of the Saints this season. If not, well, you might be picking the Lions this week. I think it’s too soon to tell what to make of New Orleans, so stay away.

The same holds true for the Commanders. Will Jayden Daniels bounce back? That aside, there’s no reason to be taking a winner in a divisional game in Week 1. You save divisional games for late in the season or maybe a Browns-type of game.

item.title: One stat that explains all 32 NFL teams entering this season
item.description: In the NFL, numbers do not tell the whole story. But they can help. As part of the SB Nation NFL preview, here is one stat or number to know for each team. In some cases it is a reflection of an area where they need to improve, for others it is a strength that […]
item.content:encoded:
In the NFL, numbers do not tell the whole story.

But they can help.

As part of the SB Nation NFL preview, here is one stat or number to know for each team. In some cases it is a reflection of an area where they need to improve, for others it is a strength that the team needs to replicate in 2026 if they are going to make a deep playoff run.

The numbers an NFL team needs are all around them.

AFC East

Buffalo Bills: 28.3

There is almost no question that the Buffalo Bills are defined by their offense.

And that 28.3 number is how many points the Bills scored per game a season ago, ranking fourth in the NFL and second in the AFC. However, they trailed the New England Patriots both in the division, and in the AFC, as the Patriots averaged 28.8 points per game.

But if the Bills are going to make the deep playoff run their fans are hoping for, they’ll need another big number in this category in 2026.

Miami Dolphins:3.37:1

This one might take some explaining.

It goes without saying that the Miami Dolphins are going through a bit of a financial makeover, and a quick scan of the team’s page on Over the Cap illustrates why. The Dolphins are paying a lot of dead cap this year — money to players no longer on the team.

Led by the more than $55 million to Tua Tagovailoa.

As such, the “3.37:1” ratio above reflects the amount of active roster cash the Dolphins are paying, to cash paid to players not on the team.

As Jason Fitzgerald of Over the Cap notes here, the league median is 97:1.

New England Patriots: 56.5

That number, 56.5, is the Adjusted Completion Percentage that Drake Maye posted on throws of 20 yards or more last regular season, as charted by Pro Football Focus. That ranked second among qualified passers last season, behind only Sam Darnold.

However, that number dipped to 36.4 in the playoffs, as the competition got tougher.

Perhaps A.J. Brown — who caught four touchdowns on those throws a season ago — can help?

New York Jets: 0

You probably know what we are referring to here.

But the 2025 New York Jets set an NFL record, becoming the first team in league history to go a full season without creating an interception.

If the preseason is any indication, this year’s squad should avoid a similar fate. The Jets snared three interceptions in the preseason, behind only the Washington Commanders and the Buffalo Bills.

AFC North

Baltimore Ravens:19%

It was a fascinating offseason for the Baltimore Ravens, who initially traded for Maxx Crosby, backed out of that deal to acquire Trey Hendrickson, signed Calais Campbell, and drafted Zion Young.

That 19% — which represents the percentage of plays where the Ravens defense pressured opposing passers last year — is a reason why. That was the fifth-lowest percentage in the league last year, and in the AFC only the New York Jets were worse.

Cincinnati Bengals:28.9

The defense in Cincinnati has been an issue for a few seasons now, including 2025. Last year the Bengals gave up a whopping 28.9 points per game, third-most in the NFL.

Cincinnati added three big names up front: Dexter Lawrence, Jonathan Allen, and Boye Mafe. Can they help bring that down to at least league average? If so, this team could finally get back to the playoffs … and save Zac Taylor’s job.

Cleveland Browns:21.0

The Cleveland Browns named Deshaun Watson as the starting quarterback to open the season.

That number, 21.0, is the QBR he posted over the seven games he started for the Browns during the 2024 season, before he suffered an Achilles injury that ended his season, and cost him the 2025 campaign.

Some around the league believe the decision is more of a two-week trial for Watson, as Cleveland begins the year with a pair of road games before their home opener in Week 3. But if Watson is going to keep his job, he’ll need to be better than that number.

Pittsburgh Steelers:6.0

That number reflects the Intended Air Yards per Passing Attempt from Aaron Rodgers last season.

It was the lowest mark of his career, since that number was first charted during the 2018 season.

It also ranked Rodgers 33rd among 33 qualified passers in the league a year ago.

Not that IAY/PA is everything, but can Rodgers push the ball downfield a bit more this season? And under Mike McCarthy?

AFC South

Houston Texans:61.7

C.J. Stroud posted a QBR of 61.7 last season.

On the one hand, it was the best single-season mark of his career, and it ranked him 12th among qualified passers in the NFL.

On the other, it was behind Mac Jones and Daniel Jones.

The defense is going to be good yet again. But can Stroud deliver this season? That might be the biggest question facing this team, and the quarterback himself, as he looks for a big-money contract extension.

Indianapolis Colts: 52%

What might this refer to?

This was the passing success rate posted by Daniel Jones last season, the highest mark of his career.

Of course, another number that could define the Colts is 44: The age of Philip Rivers when he came out of retirement to step in for an injured Daniel Jones last December.

The 2025 Colts rolled into their bye week with an 8-2 record, cementing themselves as one of the biggest surprises of the early season. But wheels came off after the buy as the Colts lost the final seven games on their schedule to finish 8-9, a stretch that included Jones’ injury and Rivers coming out of retirement.

Can Jones stay healthy this year? And if so, can he replicate that success rate again in 2026?

Jacksonville Jaguars:162

We’re zeroing in on a specific player with this number.

Specifically, Travis Hunter.

162 is the number of defensive snaps Hunter played during his rookie season, compared to the 324 he played on offense. But expect that number to increase dramatically this season, as the two-way player has focused largely on the defensive side of the ball during training camp. If he grows into the CB1 he can be, this defense should take a big step forward.

Tennessee Titans:4.6

If the Tennessee Titans are going to take a step forward in 2026, they will need a much better season from second-year passer Cam Ward.

How much better?

Well, 4.6 is the Adjusted Net Yards per Attempt that Ward delivered last season, ranking 31st out of 33 qualified passers. Only Geno Smith and J.J. McCarthy posted a lower number.

AFC West

Denver Broncos: 18.3

The 2025 Denver Broncos allowed just 18.3 points per game last year, the third-best mark in the NFL.

Can they keep that level of play this season? They’ll begin the year without Jonathon Cooper, who was placed on the Commissioner’s Exempt List, but this veteran team is largely intact from last year, with John Franklin-Myers perhaps the biggest departure, as he left for Tennessee.

Kansas City Chiefs:6.2

Last season, the league average Adjusted Net Yards per Attempt (ANY/A) among NFL passers was 6.0.

Patrick Mahomes checked in with a mark of 6.2 before his season-ending knee injury.

By all accounts, Mahomes is back healthy and ready to go in Week 1, but this will be something to watch. Quarterbacks coming back from a significant knee injury often take some time to build trust in the lower body, both while moving around in the pocket and with their throwing motion. How quickly can Mahomes get up to full speed … and how quickly can he improve on that number from last year?

Las Vegas Raiders:46.3%

While the focus in Las Vegas is on the quarterback situation, with Fernando Mendoza waiting in the wings behind newly minted starter Kirk Cousins, the Raiders have a host of questions to answer on the defensive side of the ball.

Starting with this: Can they get off the field on third downs?

Last year, the Raiders allowed third-down conversions on 46.3% of such plays, the third-most in the league. Only the Dallas Cowboys and the Carolina Panthers allowed a higher percentage of such conversions. Getting off the field on third down will help this team … and whoever is under center.

Los Angeles Chargers:27

What does that 27 represent? That is the number of games that starting tackles Joe Alt and Rashawn Slater missed last season, with Alt going down early in the year and Slater missing the entire 2025 campaign.

That led to this number: 18. That is the number of offensive line combinations the Chargers used a year ago, most in the NFL. Hopefully, that trend does not continue in Los Angeles, but losing center Tyler Biadasz for the year with a serious knee injury is not the best start …

NFC East

Dallas Cowboys: 30

That’s the number of years it’s been since the Cowboys made it to the NFC Championship Game. The Super Bowl is always the dream, but Dallas has struggled to even take a half-step and make it to the Conference Final to prove that they can be a perennial threat. Brian Schottenheimer’s first season was a step in the right direction, but there’s a long way to go.

New York Giants: 25.8 

This is how many points teams averaged against the Giants in 2025, which ranked 26th in the NFL. For all the attention that Jaxson Dart and Cam Skattebo get, it will all be for naught if this team can’t buckle down and stop the scoring. John Harbaugh has always run a tight defensive ship with a focus on the secondary, so the defensive backs getting their butts in gear will be paramount to the team’s success this year.

Philadelphia Eagles: 29.3

The length of the Eagles’ average drive in 2025 was abysmal. Ranking 25th in the NFL in yards-per-drive is unacceptable for a team with the offensive weapons Philly has, and it’s a huge factor why this team ditched Kevin Patullo as offensive coordinator. Sean Mannion brings fresh eyes to the operation, and the hope is that the explosiveness he helped bring to the Packers will breathe some life into this unit. 

Washington Commanders: 7

Jayden Daniels’ number of starts was the biggest issue for the Commanders offense in 2025, which had to limp along with Marcus Mariota under center and essentially just wait for the season to be over. There were some growing pains as Kliff Kingsbury expanded the playbook last year, but Daniels is up for the task – he just needs to stay on the field for Washington to have a shot.

NFC North

Chicago Bears: 29

Ben Johnson certainly worked wonders on the Bears’ offense in his first year as head coach, but defensively this team was bad. Ranking 29th in the NFL and allowing over 360 yards per game, it simply put too much pressure on Caleb Williams and the offense to keep bailing the Bears out. Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen needs to get more out of his unit to be a serious contender, it’s as simple as that.

Detroit Lions: 2-4

Detroit’s record against their NFC North opponents was the top reason for a down year. Inconsistency marred this team on every level in 2025 when it came to the North, as the Lions managed to go 2-0 against the Bears, but 0-2 against both the Packers, and more alarmingly, the Vikings. This team is infinitely better than it showed last season, and they will need to assert themselves inside their division before thinking about the playoffs.

Green Bay Packers: 6.9

The number of plays allowed by the Packers per drive on defense last year ranked 32nd in the NFL. This team was remarkably good at stopping teams from scoring considering that number, but it also routinely meant that the offense was marred with a bad starting position for their drives. The switch to Jonathan Gannon at defensive coordinator as Jeff Hafley goes to Miami could be addition by subtraction for the Pack.

Minnesota Vikings: 2

The number of touchdown receptions for Justin Jefferson was a career-low in 2025 as the Vikings had massive issues at quarterback for the entire season. When you look at this roster it doesn’t really matter who is under center, so long as they can get Jefferson the ball. Kyler Murray has the capability to succeed where J.J. McCarthy failed, and lift this team back up.

NFC West

Arizona Cardinals: 608

Marvin Harrison Jr. need to develop, it’s that simple. These were the number of receiving yards the young pass catcher had in 2025, and it’s getting to the point where there are real concerns whether or not he can hang in the NFL – which seemed impossible when he was drafted. There are only two goals for the Cards this season: Lose a whole lot of games, and get Harrison Jr. playing like a pro.

Los Angeles Rams: 5

That’s the number of Defensive Player of the Year awards split between Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald, who now find themselves on the same team as the Rams begin their 2026 campaign as the favorites to win the Super Bowl. While this looks incredible on paper, there’s going to be a few pain points as these two defensive legends learn to play together.

San Francisco 49ers: 194

The total number of games missed last season by the TWENTY THREE players who were placed on IR at some point during the 2025 season. That is really all that matters to this team. They just need to be healthy enough to field their top players and they’ll have a shot.

Seattle Seahawks: 1.48

The number of points scored per drive by Seahawks opponents in 2025. It was a truly unreal number that led Seattle to the NFL’s best defense. The Super Bowl Champs mostly have the same unit in place, but most-importantly, they still have Mike Macdonald, who is the architect of this whole thing.

NFC South

Atlanta Falcons: 0

The number of quarterbacks on the Falcons roster who are worth a damn. Sorry, but it’s true. Needing to settle between Tua Tagovailoa and Michael Penix Jr. is like deciding where you want to be stabbed, and that means all the pressure will be on Bijan Robinson to carry the offensive load in 2026.

Carolina Panthers: 21

This was Carolina’s rank in pass attempts last season, with the offense deciding to be much more run heavy due to a lack of weapons for Bryce Young. Outside of Tetairoa McMillan this team was lacking for a receiver for the majority of the season as Jalen Coker was hurt, and Xavier Legette underperformed. This year the Panthers need to throw the ball more, generate more explosive plays, and stop being a “run twice, throw, punt” team. 

New Orleans Saints: 4

The Saints went 6-11 on the 2025 season, but four of those wins game after the team’s bye week in November. It took time for this unit to gel together, but towards the end of the season Kellen Moore had New Orleans looking like a real football team, and more importantly: Believing they could win. Riding that wave of late-season success will define the team in 2026.

Tampa Bay Buccaneers: 14

The number of spots the Buccaneers’ scoring offense fell in 2025 as they went from being one of the league’s best units with Baker Mayfield under center, to one of the most mediocre. A lot of this was due to some key injuries, but still, the Bucs need to find ways to punch the ball into the end zone in 2026 if they hope to stay relevant in the NFC South.

item.title: Giants-Cowboys, Week 1: 5 storylines to watch
item.description: Malik Nabers’ status is the biggest story, but hardly the only one.
item.content:encoded:
The long wait for regular-season New York Giants football is nearly over. Here are five storylines to watch for Sunday’s season-opening game against the Dallas Cowboys.

Will Malik Nabers play?

The release of Darius Slayton has to be a sign that the Giants believe Nabers, their most explosive offensive player, will be ready to take the field Sunday night.

That is not guaranteed, though, as Nabers works back from a torn ACL. If he plays, how much will he play? How well will he play? How will he react to getting hit for the first time? Right now, these are all questions without answers.

How will the Giants replace Slayton?

After releasing Slayton on Monday, the Giants did not fill their open roster spot on Tuesday. Will they do so on Wednesday? Whenever they do it, who will get the 53rd roster spot?

The most obvious thing to do is replace a wide receiver with a wide receiver. That would likely mean adding either Braxton Berrios or Dalen Cambre to the 53-man roster.

If the Giants go that way, my guess would be Cambre. As a vested veteran, Berrios’ salary would be fully guaranteed for the season if he were to sign to the 53-man roster before Week 1. The Giants might want to have both on the gameday roster, and as a second-year player Cambre would cost less.

Linebacker Malik Harrison and edge defender Trace Ford could also be possibilities

Caleb Downs revenge game

Early in Harbaugh’s tenure as head coach, podcast host Mike Francesa asked him about Ohio State Caleb Downs. What Harbaugh said made just about everyone who follows the draft begin connecting Downs and the Giants.

“Big fan, big fan,” Harbaugh said of Downs. “We favor Hall of Fame safeties, so if we have a chance to draft a potential future Hall of Fame safety in Caleb Downs, that would be just fine with me.

“We’ll take the best player. You know, when you draft that high, you take the best player. It’s not a need pick. It’s the best player pick because you’re going for the guy that’s going to be that kind of a player. You’re talking about a guy that you would like to see someday wearing a gold jacket if possible. That’s what the goal is with that pick. …

That guy would be just fine with me. I’d take him in a second.”

Then, the Giants passed twice on chances to select Downs. They took linebacker Arvell Reese No. 5, and guard Sisi Mauigoa No. 10.

The Giants are quite happy with both players, with each having given indications they will live up to their draft positions.

Still, the Cowboys took Downs No. 11, meaning the Giants will have to see Downs twice a year for the foreseeable future. Will Downs make them play.

Will Tae Banks really start?

The Giants’ unofficial depth chart shows Banks as a starter instead of Paulson Adebo. Considering the way the pst two seasons went for Banks — poor play, poor tackling, poor attitude — and thew fact that Adebo is the highest-paid cornerback on the roster, Banks as a starter and Adebo as a bench player would be a stunning outcome.

That, though, appears to be what we will see on Sunday night.

Change in fortunes?

The Giants’ struggles at the beginnings of seasons have been well-documented. I wrote this a few days ago:

The Giants have begun seasons 0-2 or worse in 10 of the last 13 years.

It seems appropriate that the Giants will begin the John Harbaugh era in a nationally-televised game against the Cowboys.

The Giants and Cowboys have played seven times in season-opening games since 2012. The Giants are 1-6 in those games, with their only victory coming in 2016.

Primetime games at any time of the year have not been kind to the Giants, either.

Since 2014, the Giants are 11-36, a .234 winning percentage, in primetime.

Sunday, they get the trifecta. The Giants get the Cowboys in a primetime season-opening game.

Will things be any different this season?

item.title: The Colts’ defense is betting big on its cornerbacks staying healthy
item.description: The Colts need their cornerback group to carry a heavy load which makes the health and depth of the room worth watching.
item.content:encoded:
The Colts are going to need their cornerbacks to be one of the best position groups on the team this season. That is not really a preference as much as it is a requirement.

This defense has talent, but it also has some obvious questions. The pass rush is nothing to write home about. Laiatu Latu needs to take another step plus DeForest Buckner and Grover Stewart are still high-level interior players, but this does not look like a unit that is going to consistently overwhelm opposing quarterbacks on its own. If the pass rush is closer to average than great, the coverage has to hold up. The corners have to make quarterbacks hesitate, shrink throwing windows and most importantly buy the front extra time.

That puts a lot on Sauce Gardner, Charvarius Ward, Justin Walley and eventually Cam Taylor-Britt.

On paper, the top of the group is strong. Gardner is the star and the player this defense should be built around. Ward gives the Colts a proven veteran outside corner opposite him. Walley is expected to handle a major role in the slot and Taylor-Britt will add another experienced body once he returns from his Week 1 suspension. Taylor-Britt also possesses the ability to play outside or inside, which is key. If all of those players are available and playing well, the Colts should feel good about what they have at cornerback.

The problem is how much of that last sentence depends on “if.”

Ward is a quality corner when he is on the field, but his concussion history makes his availability one of the biggest swing factors on the defense. They need him outside, handling quality players and letting Gardner stay in his role instead of forcing the rest of the secondary to shuffle around him. If Ward misses time, the cornerback room changes quickly.

Walley brings talent and long-term upside, but he is also coming off a major injury. Asking him to step into a big role right away is already a lot. Asking him to do it while the team is thin around him adds another layer to the risk. The Colts may believe he is ready, and maybe he is, but corner is not a position where teams usually get a quiet, stress-free season from everyone involved.

Even Gardner missed games last season. That does not make him injury-prone, and it does not change the fact that he is the best player in the group, but it is another reminder that cornerback depth usually gets tested. Cornerback is a very demanding position that requires constant cutting, change of direction and full on sprinting; it is the more athletically demanding position in the entire sport. Very few teams get through a season with their top corners completely untouched.

That is why the Jaylon Jones move stands out. The Colts waived Jones while signing offensive tackle Luke Tenuta from the practice squad, which may be perfectly defensible on its own. Teams always have to balance the bottom of the roster, and offensive line depth is not something to treat lightly. Still, the move leaves the Colts light at cornerback going into Week 1, especially with Taylor-Britt suspended. Indianapolis did claim Kapena Gushiken, and there are some useful names on the practice squad, but relying on emergency elevations and new additions is not the same as having settled depth.

Jones is not some irreplaceable piece, so this is not about making his release bigger than it is. The concern is the overall bet the Colts appear willing to make. They’re asking a group with several health questions to carry a defense that needs strong coverage to function at a high level. That is a lot of pressure for a room that already feels a little thin.

The margin becomes even smaller because of what this defense is trying to cover up. If the pass rush does not consistently get home, the corners have to win longer. If the linebackers are young or slow to sort things out, the secondary has to clean up more mistakes underneath. If the safeties are still settling into new roles, communication on the back end becomes even more important. Good cornerback play can hide a lot of issues. Bad or injured cornerback play exposes everything fast. There have been many years with the Colts where the 3rd stringer is getting significant reps by the middle of the season.

That is the part that makes the health of this group so important. Gardner can change a defense by himself, but he cannot cover every receiver. Ward can raise the ceiling of the secondary, but only if he is available. Walley can become an important piece, but the Colts need him healthy and comfortable quickly. Taylor-Britt helps once he returns, but he is not available for the opener and still has to earn a role when he gets back.

The Colts are not wrong to bet on the top of their cornerback room. There is legitimate talent there, and if the group stays healthy, it should become the strength of the defense and maybe even the strength of the team. The issue is that the whole structure feels fragile. This is not a deep room loaded with proven backups. It is a talented room that needs its best players to stay on the field.

For a defense that may not have a dominant pass rush, that is a risky place to be.

If the group holds up, the defense has a chance to be much better than it was. If it does not, the Colts may find out quickly that the cornerback room was carrying more of the plan than anyone wanted to admit.

item.title: Weather forecast for Patriots’ season opener vs. Seahawks
item.description: An up-to-date weather forecast for the Wednesday game.
item.content:encoded:
The similarities between last season’s Super Bowl and this season’s regular season opener go beyond the opponents. Just like they did back in February, the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks will also square off in perfect football weather this time around.

According to NFL Weather, the kickoff temperature at Seattle’s Lumen Field on Wednesday night be 76°F with wind not expected to be a factor. A cloud cover of 99% is in the forecast but the precipitation chance is still a mere 5%.

The National Weather Service mentioned a “light and variable wind” as well as increasing clouds in its own forecast. The one shared by the Patriots via WBZ on Tuesday, meanwhile, also did not differ from any of the others.

For the Patriots, Wednesday’s game presents a continuation of the preseason conditions; their three exhibition games were all played in similar weather and kickoff temperatures in the 70s. There is one big difference, though: the starters around quarterback Drake Maye played not a single snap in the preseason. Wednesday will therefore be that particular group’s first in-game action since that Super Bowl.

The hope is that its fortunes will be different this time around from that 13-point outing resulting in a 29-13 defeat. What will effectively be the same, meanwhile, is the aforementioned weather. The stage is therefore set for a fitting opener to this year’s regular season.

Kickoff between the reigning AFC and NFC champions is scheduled for Wednesday, Sept. 9 at 8:20 p.m. ET.
